It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d383:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 February 1863. His note is document 383 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Under the formal courtesy sits real tension: a neutral Britain trading with both sides, and a Union government sure that trade kept the South alive. This exchange is where the two views met. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d483:
Document 483, dated 28 April 1863, records a letter from the State Department's chief clerk, W. Hunter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d583:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington received a letter dated 2 July 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d683:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to London on 15 December 1863, near the end of the year. His letter to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in Britain, is document 683 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume.

Year-end letters often took stock, and Washington had much to weigh. The Union held more ground, but the war was far from over, and Britain's stance still counted. Seward kept the flow of news and orders steady so Adams would not have to guess. For the reader, this note marks where the long exchange stood as 1863 closed. It gains force when read with the notes around it.
plos-pbio-0000083:
Keiichi Kondo, William Y. Kim, Mirna Lechpammer, and their team reported a cancer finding in PLOS Biology in 2003. Some kidney tumors grow after the VHL gene is lost. That loss lets a protein called HIF2α build up and push tumor growth forward.

The authors asked a sharp question: is HIF2α the main driver, or just one of many? Their tests show that blocking HIF2α alone is enough to stop these tumors from growing. That narrows a complex pathway to one key target. For drug research, the message is direct. A treatment that lowers HIF2α action might help patients whose tumors lack working VHL.
plos-pbio-0020383:
Stuart H. M. Butchart, Alison J. Stattersfield, and a huge team built a trend index for birds in PLOS Biology in 2004. The Red List ranks species by extinction risk. The team tracked how bird species move between ranks over time. From that, they made an index of whether bird life is gaining or losing.

The index fell, showing birds slipping toward extinction faster than they recovered. A single number that sums thousands of species accounts is a strong tool for policy. Governments had pledged to slow biodiversity loss, and this index lets the world check their progress. Birds were the test case, with like indices for other groups soon to follow.
plos-pone-0000083:
Domenico Girelli, Nicola Martinelli, Oliviero Olivieri, and a large team studied heart surgery outcomes in PLOS ONE in 2006. High blood levels of homocysteine, an amino acid by-product, mark a state called hyperhomocysteinemia. The team checked whether patients with high levels fared worse after coronary artery bypass grafting.

In their group, high homocysteine went with higher death rates after surgery. A blood marker that flags risk before an operation is useful: it can guide watchfulness and care after the graft. The result also adds to the long debate on homocysteine and heart disease. Whether lowering it with vitamins helps remains a separate question the data invite.
plos-pone-0000183:
Philip C. Hill, David J. Jeffries, Roger H. Brookes, and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Contacts of TB patients are checked with skin tests, but a positive result can be a false alarm. The authors use ELISPOT, a blood test that spots immune cells reacting to TB, to expose such false positive conversions.

A skin test that flips positive wrongly can trigger months of needless preventive treatment. Comparing the two tests in the same contacts shows where the skin test misleads. The work supports using blood-based tests to confirm conversions, sharpening TB control programs that track transmission through households.
plos-pone-0000283:
Mathieu Paoletti, Sven J. Saupe, and Corinne Clavé published this fungal genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fungi can tell self from non-self, rejecting tissue from genetically different individuals of the same species. The authors study the genesis, the evolutionary origin, of the repertoire of genes behind that non-self recognition.

A recognition repertoire must be diverse enough to tell many strains apart. Tracing how that diversity arose shows how fungi built an immune-like system without antibodies. The work bears on fungal biology and on the general question of how self-recognition systems evolve.
plos-pone-0000383:
Feng Chen and colleagues compared computer methods for spotting orthologs, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Orthologs are genes in different species that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. Finding them correctly is a basic step in comparing genomes and tracing how genes evolved.

Several detection strategies exist, and they do not always agree. The team assessed how well the strategies perform when applied to eukaryotic genomes, the DNA of organisms with cell nuclei, from yeast to humans. Benchmarks like this help researchers choose tools they can trust, and they show where methods still mistake look-alike genes for true counterparts.
plos-pone-0000483:
Cesare Massone and colleagues proposed an everyday device as a skin cancer screening tool, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was melanoma screening with cellular phones: using phone cameras and messaging to capture images of suspicious moles and send them for expert review.

Melanoma is curable when caught early and dangerous when late, yet dermatologists are scarce in many regions. A phone-based screen could extend expert eyes to distant patients cheaply. In 2007, phone cameras were still crude, so the idea was forward-looking. The study tested whether the images were good enough to base triage decisions on.
plos-pone-0000583:
Dinesh Adhikary and colleagues prepared immune cells aimed at a lifelong virus, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Epstein-Barr virus infects most people and hides in their cells for life. The team studied Epstein-Barr virus-specific CD4+ T cell preparations made for therapy. They asked which lytic cycle antigens dominate. In other words, which viral proteins do the therapeutic T cells mainly recognize?

Cell therapy grows a patient's own T cells against the virus and returns them, a strategy used when drugs fail. Knowing which antigens dominate the response tells makers whether their product aims at the right targets. Lytic antigens come from the virus's active phase, relevant when it reactivates in immune-suppressed patients.
plos-pone-0000683:
Marcella Funicello, Michela Novelli, Maurizio Ragni and co-authors studied mice lacking a fat-related enzyme for PLOS ONE in 2007. Proteases, proteins that cut other proteins, are implicated in fat formation and the onset of obesity. The team had reported that one cysteine protease, cathepsin K, is overexpressed in the white fat tissue of obese individuals.

Here they characterized the fat tissue of mice with the cathepsin K gene knocked out. The title states the result: during the rapid buildup of fat stores, these mice showed reduced adiposity. Linking one protease to fat gain suggests a drug target, and it reshapes how fat tissue growth is understood.
plos-pone-0000783:
Alberto Viera, Rocío Gómez, María T. Parra and colleagues watched a chromosome-shaping complex at work in mouse meiosis, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Chromosomes must be shaped and individualized so genomes segregate correctly in mitotic and meiotic divisions. In vertebrates, three multiprotein complexes drive that shaping: cohesin and condensins I and II. Meiosis, the division making sperm and eggs, has its own special chromosome choreography.

Their title promises new insights from condensin I on mouse meiotic chromosome structure and dynamics. Errors in meiosis cause infertility and conditions such as Down syndrome. Knowing which complex does what, and when, fills a basic gap in reproductive biology.
plos-pone-0000883:
Michael Lombardo, Jennifer Barnes, Sally Wheelwright and co-authors tested self-focused thought and empathy in autism, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. People on the autism spectrum often find social life hard. Whether they also differ when thinking about themselves, rather than about others, was much less clear.

The team used several well tested measures to compare self-referential cognition, thinking tied to oneself, with empathy for others. Keeping those two domains apart matters: a person can struggle with one and not the other. The study helps refine what autism affects, and what it may leave intact. That sharper picture can guide fairer tests and better support.
plos-pone-0000983:
Aparna Nittala, Soumitra Ghosh and Xujing Wang modeled how the layout of insulin cells shapes their rhythm, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Insulin leaves the pancreas in pulses, and that pulsing is basic to healthy blood sugar control. The pulses come from beta cells in each islet firing together, coupled to their neighbors.

The team built a new beta cell cluster model to ask what islet cytoarchitecture, the physical arrangement of the cells, does to the oscillation. Arrangement is easy to overlook beside chemistry. Yet if layout tunes the rhythm, then damage to islet structure in diabetes matters in its own right, not just cell loss.
plos-pone-0001083:
Dan Valente, Ilan Golani and Partha Mitra analyzed how fruit flies move in a circular arena, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Describing the full behavior of a freely moving animal is hard. Yet studies of the brain and behavior need exactly such records.

Existing metrics for movement are partial at best. They capture speed or turning, but not the whole pattern. The team present an analysis of the fly's trajectory as a complete record. Drosophila is the workhorse of genetics, so a rigorous behavior language for it serves many labs. Their approach treats the path itself as the phenotype to be explained.
plos-pone-0001183:
Diabetes often comes with reduced thyroid function and poor muscle repair after injury. Bernhard Baumgartner and colleagues went looking for a missing piece of thyroid hormone action in muscle, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They identified a gene, named DOR, that is abundant in insulin-sensitive tissues and is repressed in diabetic rat muscle.

The authors describe DOR as a novel modulator of thyroid hormone receptor-mediated action. A modulator is a protein that tunes how strongly a hormone's receptor works. Finding one that diabetes turns down connects two features of the disease, low thyroid action and weak muscle regeneration, in a single mechanism.
plos-pone-0001283:
Chuuk State, in the Federated States of Micronesia, saw its first two locally acquired HIV infections, and health officials moved to assess the risk. Toya Russell and colleagues surveyed sexual risk behaviors there, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The purpose was to assess the need for HIV education and prevention services and to develop recommendations for those services.

Remote, at-risk populations are often reached only after an epidemic is established. This study gathered first evidence before that happened in Chuuk. Its case is for early prevention fitted to a small island population.
plos-pone-0001383:
Vladimir Hampl and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a tiny single celled creature called Trimastix. Most complex cells hold small power plants called mitochondria. A few gut parasites were once thought to lack them and to have split off before such plants arose. Trimastix was one of those cases.

The team found gene proof that Trimastix did once have such power plants. Its stock of genes fits a past with them, not a past without them. That shifts where this creature sits on the tree of life. It also adds weight to the view that all complex cells share one root that held these power plants.
plos-pone-0001483:
Héctor Pálmer and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on skin growth signals. Two signals, one from the Wnt path and one from vitamin D, jointly steer how skin cells mature. Many skin genes switched on by the Wnt path carry vitamin D response marks. The team traced how the two signals share control of hair growth.

They show the vitamin D receptor acts as a Wnt effector in skin. It helps set how hair base cells mature and which tumor type forms in adult skin. That dual role was not in the standard account. It may guide new care for hair loss and skin tumors alike.
plos-pone-0001583:
Lisa Lindqvist and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the first drug aimed at one RNA helicase. Helicases unwind RNA and serve in making proteins, splicing, and RNA decay. They have little aim by nature, so blocking just one was a hard task. The team sought a drug that hits a single helicase tied to protein making.

They report a compound that does pick out that one helicase. A first in class drug proves the family can be drugged with aim. Such drugs could serve as probes, and in time as cures for ills where this helicase runs high. The work opens a new shelf in drug design.
plos-pone-0001683:
Michael J. Stringer, Marta Sales-Pardo, and Luís A. Nunes Amaral tested how well journal rankings help scientists find information, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Electronic publishing, preprint archives, blogs, and wikis had raised doubts about the place of journals and peer review. If readers can find anything online, do ranked journal lists still guide them to what matters?

The authors measured the effectiveness of ranking schemes as search tools. The full text gives their model of how scientists search, the rankings tested, and how often each scheme led readers to relevant work. The results feed a live debate about how science sorts its own flood of papers, and whether prestige rankings serve readers or mainly reward journals.
plos-pone-0001783:
Chee Gee Liew, Nadia N. Shah, Sarah J. Briston, and their co-authors pushed stem cells toward becoming insulin-making cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Human embryonic stem cells, grown as floating aggregates called embryoid bodies, differentiate into a haphazard mix of cell types from all three germ layers. Steering them to one fate is the challenge.

The team reports that PAX4, a transcription factor, enhances the differentiation of these stem cells into pancreatic beta cells. Those are the cells that make insulin and are lost in diabetes. The full text gives the culture method and the beta-cell markers. Reliable beta-cell production in the lab is a long-sought step toward cell replacement therapy for diabetes.
plos-pone-0001883:
Camille Boutin and co-authors shared a new lab method in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Their method slips genes into the brain of young mice. Testing what a gene does inside a live animal is still a core task in medical research. The front part of the brain, the forebrain, is a key site for thought and acts.

The method injects DNA into the fluid space of the brain in newborn mice, then uses a mild electric pulse to push it into cells. The team shows the trick works well in pups soon after birth. A cheap, fast way to add genes lets more labs test brain gene roles without slow breeding of mutant lines.
plos-pone-0001983:
James Curtin and co-authors sounded a caution on removing a class of immune cells in cancer therapy, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, damp down immune attack. They infiltrate glioblastoma, a deadly brain tumor, and track with tumor grade. In mice, wiping Tregs out briefly had shrunk such tumors.

The team tested Treg depletion alongside cancer immunotherapy, which tries to turn the immune system on the tumor. As the title states, depletion inhibited the therapy's efficacy instead of aiding it. That surprise matters for trial design: a step that helps alone may hurt when paired with immune therapy.
plos-pone-0002083:
Lesley Brennan and co-authors studied a bacterium that lives inside mosquito cells and shifts the host's stress defenses, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Wolbachia pipientis is an obligate inside-cell bacterium that commonly infects arthropods. Passed from mother to young, it can alter host development, sex, and reproduction in striking ways.

The team used a cell line from the mosquito Aedes albopictus that carries Wolbachia. As the title states, the endosymbiont induces the expression of host antioxidant proteins, which guard against chemical damage. A guest that raises host defenses may change how mosquitoes carry viruses, a trait vector control hopes to use.
plos-pone-0002183:
Fang Tang, Wei Liu, Fang Zhang, and co-authors looked for gene variants that change the risk of SARS, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. SARS, severe acute respiratory syndrome, swept through China and beyond in 2003. Cytokines, the immune system's signal proteins, play key roles in fighting viruses, so genes that tune them may shape who gets badly ill.

The team ran a case-control study in Chinese SARS patients, focusing on variants in the gene for the IL-12 receptor, IL-12RB1. They report that some variants add to a person's chance of catching SARS or faring worse. Such findings help explain why the same virus strikes some people far harder than others.
plos-pone-0002283:
Yasuhide Iwata, Katsuaki Suzuki, Tomoyasu Wakuda, and co-authors tested whether radiation in adult rats can model schizophrenia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Population studies had suggested that radiation exposure may be a risk factor for schizophrenia in adult humans. No animal model had directly tested that link with adult exposure.

The team gave adult rats a total dose of 15 gray of irradiation in six fractions and checked their behavior. They looked for abnormalities relevant to schizophrenia, such as changes in activity and response to startling sounds. A radiation-based model, if it holds, would give researchers a new handle on how this illness can arise in adult life.
plos-pone-0002383:
McGrath led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are John McGrath, Takeshi Iwazaki, Darryl Eyles, among others. Its subject is protein Expression in the Nucleus Accumbens of Rats Exposed to Developmental Vitamin D Deficiency. Developmental vitamin D (DVD) deficiency is a candidate risk factor for schizophrenia.

Animal models have confirmed that DVD deficiency is linked to a range of altered genomic, proteomic, structural and behavioural outcomes in the rat. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002483:
Gennaro and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Luigi De Gennaro, Fabiana Fratello, Cristina Marzano, among others. Its subject is cortical Plasticity Induced by Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation during Wakefulness Affects Electroencephalogram Activity during Sleep. Sleep electroencephalogram (EEG) brain oscillations in the low-frequency range show local signs of homeostatic regulation after learning.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002583:
El-Bchiri joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Jamila El-Bchiri, Agathe Guilloux, Peggy Dartigues, among others. Its subject is nonsense-Mediated mRNA Decay Impacts MSI-Driven Carcinogenesis and Anti-Tumor Immunity in Colorectal Cancers. Nonsense-mediated mRNA Decay (NMD) degrades mutant mRNAs containing premature termination codon (PTC-mRNAs).

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002683:
Mogens Kilian and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on evolution of streptococcus pneumoniae and its close commensal relatives. The catalog record names Mogens Kilian first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a member of the Mitis group of streptococci which, according to 16S rRNA-sequence based phylogenetic reconstruction, includes 12 species. It goes on to note a further point. While other species of this group are considered prototypes of commensal bacteria, S. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002783:
Jean-Jacques Parienti and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was not all missed doses are the same: sustained NNRTI treatment interruptions predict HIV rebound at Low-to-Moderate adherence levels. Authorship is credited in the record to Jean-Jacques Parienti and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. While the relationship between average adherence to HIV potent antiretroviral therapy is well defined. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002883:
Giovanna Vinci, Xuhua Xia and Reiner A. Veitia asked in PLOS ONE in 2008 why some animals keep genes they no longer seem to need. Enzymes that build sterols are much alike across species that make sterols from scratch. Yet two animals that cannot make cholesterol still kept copies of the matching genes.

Those animals are called cholesterol auxotrophs, meaning they must get cholesterol from food. The paper weighs facts and possible reasons for the genes staying in place. It may be that the genes now serve other jobs. The puzzle helps readers think about how genomes shed, or keep, old tools.
plos-pone-0002983:
Haichun Gao, Donna Pattison, Tingfen Yan and co-authors built a clone collection for the bacterium Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 in 2008. They constructed the set with a recombinase cloning system that lets genes be moved between plasmids with ease. In total, 3,584 individual genes, about 85 percent, were cloned successfully.

To validate the set, three groups of genes were tested in protein expression and phage display. Published in PLOS ONE, the resource serves work on a bacterium prized for breathing metals and cleaning polluted sites. Shared clone sets save every lab from rebuilding the same tools. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003083:
Giuseppe Pagnoni, Milos Cekic and Ying Guo scanned the brains of Zen meditators in 2008. Brain imaging had identified a default network active during wakeful rest that deactivates during demanding tasks. That network was linked to the stream of thoughts running through the mind at rest.

Their study, titled around thinking about not-thinking, examines conceptual processing during Zen meditation. Published in PLOS ONE, meditators offer a trained case of quieting that stream. The work tests how a practiced mind handles the default network differently. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003183:
Thomas L. Turner, Eric J. von Wettberg and Sergey V. Nuzhdin search for local adaptation genes in a rockcress in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serpentine soil is naturally high in heavy metals and has a low calcium to magnesium ratio, making a difficult home for most plants. Yet many species live only on serpentine, and many wider taxa have been shown to adapt to it.

The team analyse genomic differences between soil types in Arabidopsis lyrata to reveal candidate genes for local adaptation. Readers see adaptation traced to specific genome regions. The work helps explain how plants colonize harsh soils that would poison most species.
plos-pone-0003283:
Digna R. Velez, Stephen J. Fortunato, Poul Thorsen and colleagues link gene variants to preterm birth in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Spontaneous preterm birth, before thirty-seven weeks, occurs in about twelve percent of pregnancies in the United States and is the largest contributor to neonatal morbidity and mortality. Preterm birth is a complex disease potentially induced by several causes from multiple pathways.

The title reports that preterm birth in Caucasians is associated with coagulation and inflammation pathway gene variants. Readers see two biological routes, clotting and inflammation, tied genetically to early birth. Such variants may help identify pregnancies needing closer care.
plos-pone-0007383:
Ombretta Caspani, Sandra Zurborg, Dominika Labuz, and colleagues studied cold pain sensors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Cold allodynia is enhanced sensitivity to cold, a common feature of neuropathic pain. Its underlying mechanisms were not known, leaving patients with few targeted treatments for this disabling symptom after nerve injury.

Two channels, TRPM8 and TRPA1, had been proposed as molecular cold sensors. The authors test the contribution of both channels to cold allodynia and neuropathic pain. Their experiments separate the roles of the two sensors. Knowing which channel drives cold pain could focus drug development.
plos-pone-0007483:
Mailyn Gonzalez and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on naming the trees of the Amazon rainforest. Conservation planning depends on large inventories of plant diversity. Classic taxonomy, naming species by eye, is slow and expert-hungry. That bottleneck is worst in megadiverse tropical forests. The team tested DNA barcodes, short genetic tags, as a faster way to identify trees from a detailed forest census.

Working from a census of the study forest's trees, they checked how reliably barcodes could name them. Genetic tags matched many trees to their correct species. The approach will not replace taxonomists, but it can scale surveys far beyond hand identification. Faster inventories mean conservation choices can rest on fuller counts of what is actually there. The study is a field test of barcoding where diversity is highest.
plos-pone-0007583:
Shibing Yu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how parathyroid hormone builds bone. The hormone is a potent treatment for osteoporosis because it stimulates new bone rather than only slowing loss. Its mechanism inside bone-forming cells was not well understood. The team tested mice lacking a protein called activating transcription factor 4, or ATF4. They gave the hormone to growing and adult animals and measured the response.

Without ATF4, the hormone's bone-building action was severely impaired. That makes ATF4 a critical link in the chain from hormone signal to new bone. Knowing the link refines how the therapy is understood. It may also suggest ways to strengthen the treatment or mimic it. For a disease that thins the skeletons of millions, each part of the building machinery matters.
plos-pone-0007683:
Nicholas Levinson, Patrick Visperas and John Kuriyan published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on an enzyme called Csk. Csk belongs to a set of enzymes that switch other proteins on or off by adding a phosphate group. Its own activity is tuned by two key sites on related enzymes.

The authors show that Csk joins with a second Csk molecule to form a pair. The pairing happens through a part of the protein called the SH3 domain. How enzymes pair up can change how strongly they work. This detail helps explain how Csk is controlled inside the cell.
plos-pone-0007783:
Herman Pontzer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses the physics of running to test whether two-legged dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Whether dinosaurs were endothermic, ectothermic or in between is a classic unsettled question. The answer also bears on when warm-bloodedness arose on the line to birds.

Running costs energy, and warm-blooded animals can sustain far higher energy output. The authors calculated the metabolic demands of running for bipedal dinosaurs. Their biomechanics point toward endothermy in these animals. Physics thus joins fossils and growth rings as evidence on dinosaur physiology.
plos-pone-0007883:
Alejandra Delprat and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how a jumping gene can flip a chunk of chromosome in fruit flies. Jumping genes, or transposons, are known sources of chromosomal inversions. Flies carry many inversions, both within species and between them.

Direct evidence for how inversions arise in flies was thin. The team traced inversions to the transposon they named Galileo. Copies of Galileo at two sites can recombine in the wrong pairing, flipping the segment between them. The mechanism explains a common kind of genome change. It helps connect mobile DNA to evolution.
plos-pone-0007983:
Siming Liu and colleagues linked insulin signals to cell power plants in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their stage was the pancreatic beta cell, the cell that makes insulin. Inside it they found a complex that ties mitochondria, the power plants, close to the sugar-sensing machinery.

With that tie in place, insulin signals could tune how the power plants work. A beta cell must sense sugar, make energy, and release insulin in step; the tie helps join those jobs. The find adds a layer to how these cells keep blood sugar in range, and where that control may fail in diabetes.
plos-pone-0008083:
Lucia Marucci and colleagues gave recipes for turning a gene circuit into a clock or a switch in PLOS ONE in 2009. Synthetic biologists build small circuits from gene parts and want them to behave as planned. Two prized behaviors are steady ticking and clean flipping between two states.

Using math models, the team showed how tweaks to one basic circuit yield each behavior, and how to tune the tick or the flip. Recipes like these bring built biology closer to the trust we place in built electronics, where parts do what the diagram promises.
plos-pone-0008183:
Jonathan C. Schisler and co-authors explored ancestry and metabolism in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. People of African descent in the United States face higher rates of obesity and diabetes. They also face more hypertension and heart disease linked to those conditions. The team asked whether gene activity tied to carbohydrate use differs by geographic ancestry.

Using a combined approach, the authors looked for stable patterns of gene expression. Stable patterns are ones that hold up across samples and conditions. If ancestry shapes how the body handles sugars, that could help explain unequal disease rates. It could also guide more precise study of metabolic disease.
plos-pone-0008283:
Ruchika Srinivasan and colleagues studied blood vessel growth in mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2009. Angiogenesis builds new vessels through a complex, stepwise process. Endothelial cells first break through the vessel wall, then migrate and multiply. The Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK pathway is required for endothelial cell function. Within it, Erk1 and Erk2 are close partner proteins.

The team asked how each partner regulates cell proliferation and migration. Separating their roles matters for understanding vessel development. It also matters for diseases where vessel growth goes wrong. The study maps part of the signaling chain behind embryonic angiogenesis.
plos-pone-0008383:
Julie Tenenbaum and colleagues studied mutant hormone receptors in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Some patients have the nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, or NSIAD. They carry mutations in the V2 receptor, at positions named R137C or R137L. The mutant receptors are constitutively active, switched on without their hormone. Clinical features were known, but molecular mechanisms remained elusive.

The team found these mutants respond only weakly to agonist and antagonist regulation. Drugs that normally raise or block the receptor lose much of their grip. That explains features of the syndrome. It also shapes treatment expectations for patients.
plos-pone-0008483:
Duarte Viana and co-authors test cooperation in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. They use a social game based on the Prisoner's Dilemma. In that game, working together pays both players, but each is tempted to defect. Game theory has long used the dilemma to study reciprocity. The team ask what rats need, in mind and motive, for cooperation to emerge in play.

Rats face the game with a partner over repeated rounds. The authors vary what rats can learn and expect from partners. Cooperation grows only when those conditions are met. The study helps explain when simple animals can sustain shared, costly help.
plos-pone-0008583:
Teal Hallstrand and co-authors profile genes in asthma in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. One common form is triggered by exercise. It occurs in many people with asthma. During attacks, the airways release lipid signals that drive swelling. The team measure gene activity across the genome in distinct asthma types. They seek genes that are more active in the exercise form.

They find an enzyme called TG2 is a new regulator of those lipid signals. TG2 had not been linked to this path before. It is a fresh target for drugs to curb exercise attacks. Sorting asthma by type reveals drivers that pooled studies miss.
plos-pone-0008683:
Michael Russello, Nikos Poulakakis, James Gibbs, and colleagues reported a happy surprise from the Galápagos. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study concerns a tortoise kind long thought extinct. The species once lived only on one island and vanished from the wild. Old DNA, drawn from museum bones, gave the team a reference.

Captive tortoises held far from home carried genes matching that lost species. In other words, descendants of the extinct kind still live in zoos and collections. Breeders could use those animals to rebuild a wild population. The case shows how old DNA can steer modern rescue work.
plos-pone-0008783:
Hai-Guo Zhang, Yao-Fong Chen, Ming Ding, and colleagues completed a fingerprint survey of all Chinese ethnic groups. Their huge project appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dermatoglyphics is the study of finger and palm ridge patterns. Such patterns form before birth and never change. A full survey of a diverse country was once thought nearly impossible. Teams across China gathered the data over many years.

Ridge measures varied in clear geographic patterns across groups. Northern and southern populations showed their own signatures. The completed map serves anthropology, genetics, and medical studies. It stands as a reference atlas of human variation in China.
plos-pone-0008883:
Mirjam Metzner, Wolfgang Schuh, Edith Roth, and colleagues sorted an antibody-editing enzyme into two forms. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, AID, mutates antibody genes in B cells on purpose. Those mutations let antibodies sharpen their grip on germs. Hunting for AID's partner proteins is a standard research route. Oddly, the enzyme behaved inconsistently in a common lab material, agarose.

Two forms of AID differed in how they bound that material. Separating the forms clears up confusing partner hunts. Form differences may also reflect real regulation inside B cells. Antibody science gains a cleaner picture of its key mutator.
plos-pone-0008983:
Caia Duncan and Kevin Weeks mapped how a helper protein grips a self-cutting RNA in yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some RNA molecules, called ribozymes, can cut and rejoin themselves. The bI3 intron in yeast mitochondria is one of them, but it works poorly alone. It needs two proteins, and one of them is the splicing factor Mrs1.

The team found Mrs1 holds the intron at two separate grip points. Each grip is a tetraloop-receptor motif, a small folded shape in the RNA. Holding both points likely folds the intron into its working shape. Mrs1 began as a DNA-cutting enzyme family member, later retrained for RNA work.
plos-pone-0009083:
Matthew Henn and co-authors compared ways of reading and labelling the genomes of phages, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Phages are viruses that infect bacteria and steer whole ecosystems. They kill hosts and shuttle genes between them. Despite that importance, phage genomes were poorly charted when the study ran.

High-throughput sequencing had just made reading many phage genomes cheap. The team tested strategies for sequencing and for annotating what the genes do. Different pipelines gave different completeness and accuracy. Their comparison offers a practical guide for labs entering phage genomics.
plos-pone-0009183:
Kathryn Chu and co-authors published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It follows HIV patients in a primary care treatment program in South Africa. At the time, most African programs used a fixed-dose drug mix containing nevirapine. Doctors worried that nevirapine could damage the liver early in treatment.

The team measured how often early liver harm occurred in the program. They also looked for patient traits that raised the risk, and counted deaths linked to the damage. Such numbers matter because programs had to weigh nevirapine's benefits against its dangers. The findings helped clinicians decide who needed closer liver checks when starting treatment.
plos-pone-0009283:
Linda Ferencko and Boris Rotman published this spore engineering study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacillus spores are among the toughest objects in biology. Each spore wears a coat built from about sixty different proteins. That coat was long seen as static armor, giving the spore its rigidity and protection.

The authors decorated coat proteins with water-repelling chemical groups. The treatment made the spores glow under the right light, creating fluorogenic spores. Glowing spores can be tracked as they move through soil, water, or instruments. The trick turns a passive survival capsule into a useful tracer for science and industry.
plos-pone-0011383:
Pramod Dash and colleagues tested in 2010 whether a long-used epilepsy drug could protect the brain after a severe injury. A blow to the head kills brain cells not only at impact but over the hours that follow, and few drugs can slow that second wave. The team gave valproate to rats after a traumatic brain injury and compared them with untreated rats.

Treated animals lost fewer brain cells and did better on tests of thinking and memory. An approved drug with a known safety record showing this benefit is valuable, since it could reach patients faster than a brand-new compound. The study supports trials of valproate as an early treatment after head injury. It also suggests that calming certain cell pathways soon after trauma can save tissue that would otherwise be lost.
plos-pone-0011483:
Antonia Kalushkova and co-authors reported in 2010 that a set of development genes is switched off in multiple myeloma. Myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow, and its gene control is badly scrambled. The Polycomb system is a master silencer that keeps embryo genes off in adult cells, and its normal targets should be handled with care in blood cells.

In myeloma, genes targeted by Polycomb were found silenced, a pattern pointing to hijacked developmental controls helping drive the cancer. Silencing the wrong set can lock cells in an immature, ever-dividing state. The finding matters because drugs that undo abnormal silencing already exist for other cancers. If myeloma's silencing pattern is a driver rather than a bystander, those epigenetic drugs deserve testing against it, guided by the pattern itself.
plos-pone-0011583:
Krishna Kumar Veeravalli and co-authors studied human glioma cells, a form of aggressive brain tumour, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Three helpers called MMP-9, uPAR and cathepsin B are known to aid tumour spread. They help cancer cells stick, move, invade nearby tissue and grow new tumours elsewhere.

Using short RNA tools, the team switched off all three helpers in tumour cells grown in dishes and in mice. Levels of integrins, the proteins cells use to grip their surroundings, then fell sharply. Weakening several helpers at once may therefore slow glioma spread, and the work points to combined targets for future treatment.
plos-pone-0011783:
Mareike Fett and co-authors tested a guard protein in a zebrafish model of Parkinson's disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in the gene for parkin cause most cases of the inherited, early form of the disease. Mice that lack parkin, though, show little brain harm, which left researchers with no good living model of its guard role.

In engineered zebrafish, parkin held off protein-poison stress, the harm done by misfolded proteins that pile up in cells. The fish test backs the guard's protective role in a living animal. Small zebrafish may also give a faster test bed for Parkinson's drugs than mice.
plos-pone-0011883:
Yimo Liu and Diane Bassham showed in 2010 that a growth regulator also restrains recycling inside plant cells. The regulator is TOR, a protein that senses nutrient conditions. The recycling process is autophagy, in which cells break down and reuse their own contents during stress or aging.

Working in Arabidopsis thaliana, the small plant used in labs worldwide, the team found TOR acting as a negative regulator, holding autophagy down. The same broad control had been seen in animals, so the plant result suggests an ancient, shared switch. Understanding that switch matters for how plants survive hunger and how their aging leaves are dismantled.
plos-pone-0011983:
Rajwahrdhan Yadav and co-workers described in 2010 an odd effect of whooping cough toxin on immune replies to the body's own tissues. The toxin is most known for making self-attack diseases worse in lab animals, boosting models of eye and brain disease in which the immune system turns on the self. How it does that boosting is still argued about.

Yet in this study the toxin held back a slow, cell-led immune reply to self proteins in mice, the flip side of its usual name. A tool long used to stir up self-attack acting as a brake in a new setup warns against one-line tales about immune drugs. Dose, timing, and place all matter, and the work pushes labs to state those terms before they call a drug a booster or a brake.
plos-pone-0012083:
Luis Fernandes and co-workers used in 2010 a branch of math born of phone lines and codes. With it they audited the maps that chart how proteins touch each other in the cell. Those maps are built from tests of many kinds, and each kind has its own blind spots and quirks. The team brought in scales from that math to sum up each map's shape in a few firm traits.

Read with those scales, the maps showed two things at once. One was warps left by the tests that made them. The other was traits that stay the same from one kind of life to the next. Telling warp from truth is a must before such maps are mined for drug aims. The scales also give the field a way to check its own work, map by map.
plos-pone-0012183:
Ming Li, Dankyu Yoon, Jong-Young Lee, and co-authors tested smoking-linked gene variants in a Korean population for PLOS ONE in 2010. A cluster of nicotine receptor genes on chromosome fifteen had been tied to nicotine dependence in many large studies, but nearly all those studies drew on people of European descent. Whether the same variants matter in Asian populations was an open question.

The team checked the cluster's variants against smoking behaviors in Korean subjects. Confirming or refuting the link in a new population decides whether the finding is a general human trait or a local one. Such cross-population checks keep genetics honest and can sharpen the search for what makes quitting so hard.
plos-pone-0012283:
Robert Jenkins, Rasha Bennagi, John Martin, and co-authors found a folded switch controlling a growth factor's production, in PLOS ONE in 2010. TGF-beta 1 steers cell growth, movement, and survival across the body, yet its message is notoriously reluctant to be translated into protein. That reluctance is itself a control point, lifted under certain stimuli.

The team pinned the control to a conserved stem-loop shape in the message's opening region. A shape-based switch explains how cells can keep the message ready yet silent until needed. Since too much of this factor drives scarring and helps cancers, its translation switch is a plausible drug target that DNA-level studies would never have shown.
plos-pone-0012383:
Osbaldo Resendis-Antonio, Alberto Checa and Sergio Encarnación charted the core metabolism of cancer cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cancer cells burn sugar in a wasteful way even when oxygen is plentiful, a quirk called the Warburg effect, and they pour building blocks into new amino acids, fats, and DNA parts. The authors mapped the network of reactions that sustains this growth mode.

By surveying the layout of the network, they highlight the hubs and backup routes that let tumor cells keep growing. A map like this shows where a drug might starve a tumor and where the cell could reroute around a block. It gives drug hunters a systems view rather than one enzyme at a time.
plos-pone-0012483:
León Martínez-Castilla and Rogelio Rodríguez-Sotres proposed a quality score for computer-built protein models, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Predicting a protein's three-dimensional fold from its sequence remains a central problem, because shape decides function. Modelers need a trustworthy way to grade a predicted shape before trusting it.

Their score asks how well a model can retrieve its own sequence when the sequence is threaded back onto the shape. A good fold should welcome its true sequence more than others. Such self-consistency checks give modelers a cheap internal grade, useful when no experimental structure exists to compare against, which is most of the time.
plos-pone-0012583:
Wiebke Mohr, Tobias Großkopf, Douglas Wallace and colleagues checked whether standard methods undercount ocean nitrogen fixation, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Fixing nitrogen gas into usable forms feeds ocean life and the global nitrogen budget. Two methods dominate measurement: a tracer addition test and the acetylene reduction assay, and their results often disagree.

The team found methodological reasons the tracer method can underestimate true fixation rates. Undercounted fixation means ocean productivity and carbon uptake models rest on low numbers. Correcting the method ripples through climate science, since the ocean's nitrogen supply limits how much carbon marine life can draw down.
plos-pone-0012683:
Sughra, Birbach, de Martin and co-authors traced contacts between three proteins in the inflammation pathway. The pathway centres on NF-kappa B, a switch for genes of inflammation and cell survival. One key enzyme in it is IKK2, and helper proteins called TRAFs shape its action.

Their 2010 study showed TRAF1 binding both IKK2 and TRAF2, hinting it regulates the pathway. A regulator sitting between two known players gives drug hunters another handle on inflammation. Unchecked NF-kappa B drives many diseases, so each control point counts. Fine wiring of this kind is what drug design builds on.
pmc-3441783:
Teixeira, Carraca, Markland, and co-authors review exercise research in a planned way through the lens of self-determination theory. Motivation is a critical factor in keeping exercise going over time. Sustained activity, in turn, is linked to important health outcomes.

Research using this theory of motivation had grown sharply in recent years. The review gathers that work to ask which forms of motivation best predict lasting activity. Its answer favours enjoyment and personal value over pressure and guilt. Programme designers use those findings to build exercise schemes people stick with.  Enjoyment-based programmes retained participants longer than those built on external rewards alone.
pmc-3701683:
Xia, Wang, and He present BrainNet Viewer, a network visualisation tool for human brain connectomics. The brain is a complex system, and its organisation can be represented as a network of connected regions. Studies had shown that such connectomes can be built from various brain imaging technologies.

Sophisticated analytic methods can then characterise those networks, but researchers still need clear pictures to grasp them. BrainNet Viewer renders brain networks in three dimensions, showing nodes and connections together. Visual tools like it help neuroscientists share and compare findings about brain wiring.
pmc-3789683:
Chaimani, Higgins, Mavridis, and co-authors present graphical tools for network meta-analysis in the STATA statistics package. Network meta-analysis synthesises direct and indirect evidence across trials that compare multiple treatments. It has the potential to rank competing treatments for a given outcome.

Despite its usefulness, the approach is often criticised, partly because results are hard to display and check. Their graphs show the network of comparisons and where evidence is strong or thin. Clearer pictures help readers judge whether treatment rankings rest on solid ground.  Forest-style plots in the paper show how indirect evidence shifts treatment rankings.
pmc-5210583:
Forbes, Beare, Boutselakis, and their co-authors updated COSMIC in 2016. COSMIC catalogues the somatic mutations found in human cancer at fine detail, letting users explore targets and trends in cancer genetics. It was already the widest store of cancer mutations anywhere.

Expert curators build its content from published studies and large cancer genome projects. Users can trace which mutations recur in each cancer type and how often. Recurrent mutations point to genes that drive cancer growth. Oncologists and researchers use that knowledge to classify tumors, choose targeted drugs, and design new studies of cancer genetics.
pmc-5605883:
The GBD 2016 Causes of Death Collaborators reported in 2017 on mortality by cause worldwide. Tracking who dies early, and whether those rates rise or fall, is key to cutting premature death. The study behind the report, GBD 2016, assesses deaths by cause in full for this purpose.

The analysis covers cause-specific mortality for hundreds of causes in nearly two hundred locations, by age and sex, from 1980 to 2016. It reveals which causes retreat, such as many infections, and which advance, such as dementias. Governments and funders use these trends to judge whether health programs work. The dataset is the reference scoreboard for global mortality.
pmc-6252083:
The GBD 2017 DALYs and HALE Collaborators published this disability analysis in 2018. It measures not just how long people live, but how much of that life is spent in poor health. Those patterns shape policy, planning, and care services.

The study reports disability-adjusted life years for a long list of diseases and injuries across most countries. Back pain, headache, and depression rank among the top causes of years lived unwell. As deaths fall, nonfatal burdens take a larger share. The findings argue for health systems built for chronic care, not only for saving lives.
pmc-6425583:
Alexander Wolf, Fiona Hamey, Mireya Plass, and coauthors introduced PAGA for single-cell data in 2019. Single-cell RNA data hold both distinct cell types and smooth transitions between them. Older methods forced a choice between grouping cells and ordering them along paths.

PAGA builds a graph that shows how cell groups connect, keeping the overall shape of the data. That map can then guide detailed trajectory fitting within each branch. The result reads like a subway map of cell development. Analysts use it to reconcile cluster labels with the continuous nature of real differentiation.
pmc-7689983:
Hyuk Sung Kwon and Seong-Ho Koh reviewed in 2020 how inflammation inside the brain drives diseases that slowly destroy nerve cells. Such neuroinflammation accompanies conditions including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Two kinds of support cells, microglia and astrocytes, act as the main controllers of inflammation in the central nervous system.

The authors explain how these cells normally protect neurons, and how their activation can turn harmful and feed the disease process. They survey the signals that pass between the two cell types and the rest of the brain. Understanding this switch from defense to damage is central to the search for treatments that slow these diseases rather than merely easing their symptoms.
pmc-7778883:
Ivica Letunic, Supriya Khedkar, and Peer Bork reported in 2020 the latest state of SMART, a web tool for studying the building blocks of proteins. Proteins are assembled from domains, reusable parts that each carry a function. SMART lets researchers identify those domains in a protein and map how they are arranged along it.

The update describes new additions and the status of the resource, whose ninth version holds carefully curated models for well over a thousand protein domains. The authors explain how the models are built and checked by hand. Resources like SMART turn a raw protein sequence into a readable plan, which is often the first step in guessing what an unknown protein does.
pmc-8689983:
Marc Gillespie and colleagues described the 2022 state of the Reactome pathway knowledgebase, a free resource that maps the chemical reactions of human biology. Reactome records, in expert checked detail, how molecules interact across a wide range of normal and disease processes. It covers inherited conditions as well as illnesses acquired through life.

The article reports the growth of the database and the tools for exploring it, from pathway diagrams to analysis of a user's own data. Every pathway is curated by hand from the published literature, which keeps the detail trustworthy. Biologists consult Reactome when they need to know not just which genes changed, but which chain of reactions those changes belong to.
pmc-8728283:
Fiona Cunningham and colleagues presented Ensembl 2022, the annual report of a genome resource now serving all eukaryotic life, not only vertebrates. Ensembl annotates genomes, marking genes, regulatory regions, and variation, and it is built to deliver that annotation at very large scale. For key species such as humans and farm animals, the annotation runs especially deep.

The article describes recent growth in species coverage, data types, and access routes, including rapid release tracks for new genomes. It also explains the infrastructure that keeps the service flexible for very different kinds of users. Ensembl's yearly reports double as a census of how far genome annotation has spread across the tree of life.
pmc-9034083:
Kai Hou and co-authors reviewed in 2022 the roles of the microbiota, the communities of microbes living on and in the body, in health and disease. Since microbes were first linked to wellbeing, study after study has widened their importance. The authors sort these communities by where they live: gut, mouth, airways, and skin.

Each community lives in a working partnership with its host, and each can fall out of balance in characteristic ways. The review describes what each community does when healthy and the diseases tied to its disruption. It gives readers one map of a body-wide system that medicine increasingly treats as an organ in its own right.
plos-pone-0357883:
Zhongbao Zuo and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It compares two ways of assessing liver fibrosis, scarring of the liver, in patients in China who live with chronic liver disease: FibroTouch, an ultrasound-based device, and CHI3L1, a blood marker. The title claims FibroTouch diagnoses better and costs less.

Staging fibrosis decides treatment urgency, yet biopsy, the old standard, is invasive and costly. A device that is both more accurate and cheaper than a blood test would simplify clinic work greatly. Liver specialists and hospital purchasers in China are the readers weighing this head-to-head claim.
plos-pone-0359583: Pang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on two common joint and bone diseases. They merged public data, starting from the diseases rather than from single genes. A computer-based knockout test then ranked proteins shared by worn joints and thinning bones. Those shared proteins are prime suspects for why the two diseases often strike the same people, and they may guide new treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0358983: Cheng and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on recovery after a major heart attack type called STEMI. They read gene signals in blood samples and built a single-cell atlas of the cells involved. The title reports their main hint: one cell family, the monocytes, sits on an axis between recovery and failure. That axis may help doctors predict who will heal well.
plos-pone-0359283: Yaikwawong and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on spotting early metabolic trouble in Thai adults. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risks like high blood sugar and belly fat. The team used machine learning with routine clinic measures to sort pre-syndrome cases from full cases. A cheap sort from standard tests could flag people early, before diabetes or heart disease sets in.
plos-pone-0358483:
Farhan Naeem and four colleagues pit two modern object detection systems against each other on brain scans, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Finding a tumor's exact location on magnetic resonance images is a step toward early diagnosis and treatment planning. The team compared a convolution based detector, YOLOv11s, with a transformer based rival, RF-DETR, on the same annotated scan collection.

YOLOv11s came out ahead on the headline measures, with detection quality, precision, and recall all a few points higher. The transformer model held one advantage: it located tumors more tightly when judged by stricter overlap standards. The authors note the hard part was fairness, since the two systems learn features differently and train under different settings. The comparison gives imaging teams a grounded basis for choosing between the two families.
