plos-pone-0358883:
Kimberly Smart leads a team of eight asking whether severe chronic hives foreshadow other immune diseases, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Chronic spontaneous urticaria brings wheals and swelling for months without a clear trigger, and its moderate to severe form needs immune suppressing or biologic drugs. Using a large American health records network spanning 2014 to 2026, the team matched over sixteen thousand such patients with the same number of mild cases.

The severe group went on to develop rheumatoid arthritis at clearly higher rates, and Sjögren's syndrome, an immune attack on tear and saliva glands, was also significantly more common. The comparison adjusted for age, sex, background, and family history, and survived strict statistical correction. Association is not causation, but the pattern suggests doctors treating stubborn hives should stay alert for joint and gland symptoms that signal a second immune condition emerging.
plos-pone-0357783:
Vamsi Krishna Kudapa leads a team of eight greening the mud that lubricates oil and gas drilling, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Drilling fluids must carry rock cuttings up the hole and seal the well wall, but conventional additives raise environmental objections. Ten water based formulations were mixed with three candidate additives at several doses: pistachio shell powder, magnesium oxide nanoparticles, and carbon black, then tested for thickness, flow behavior, and fluid loss.

The pistachio powder, an agricultural waste, won on balance. It raised the mud's lifting strength and gel quality. It kept density and acidity steady. It also formed a thin sealing cake that limited fluid loss better than carbon black, and comparably to the engineered nanoparticles. All the muds thinned under shear as drilling requires. The authors pitch shell powder as that rare green substitute that sacrifices nothing in performance while costing less than its synthetic rivals.
plos-pone-0355783:
Zhenshui Yan and three colleagues wire shoppers' brains to watch green packaging decisions happen, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Delivery packaging can be sold in greener form at a premium, and advertisers frame the choice either as good for the planet or good for the buyer. Combining behavior tests with scalp recorded brain waves, the team varied the price premium and the advertising appeal, then tracked two signals: an early conflict wave and a late evaluation wave.

Price ruled. As the premium rose, green choices fell sharply, whatever the advertisement said. Brain signals showed why: high premiums triggered stronger early conflict, worst of all under self interested appeals. Under a small premium, planet framed appeals boosted the late wave tied to moral satisfaction. Past a personal price threshold, that boost vanished entirely. Green marketing, the authors conclude, works only inside a price window set by the wallet, not the conscience.
plos-pone-0356883:
Muhammad Fahmi Ahmad Zuber led a team of four authors reviewing how to prevent harmful drug mixes, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Poor prescribing can pair drugs that should never meet, with risks from bleeding to organ failure. The team reviewed efforts that try to cut such interactions, both fixed-rule and chance-based approaches.

Zuber's review weighed which kinds of intervention actually reduce dangerous pairings in real practice. Alerts alone often get ignored, so evidence on what works beyond alerts matters. Hospitals and clinics can use the synthesis to pick strategies with proof behind them. Safer prescribing protects patients who take many medicines at once, most often older adults with several conditions.
plos-pone-0356783:
Christopher Wolsko and Elizabeth Marino tested a fresh approach to vaccine messages in the United States, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their idea was to affirm the public's own values inside health communications, rather than lecture from authority. They measured whether that approach changes plans to get a vaccine, and how far people trust the message.

Wolsko and Marino ran their test with U.S. participants and tracked both intentions and trust. Work like this matters because vaccine uptake depends on trust as much as on facts. If affirming a person's values opens the mind, health agencies gain a low-cost tool for campaigns. The study gives communicators evidence on a tone choice they make every day.
plos-pone-0355683:
Matteo A Ruberto and three colleagues studied parenthood in academic careers, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Having children changes how scholars work, and the effect is known to differ for mothers and fathers. The team compared publication counts with how productive scholars judge themselves to be.

Ruberto's group documented where the parenthood penalty falls hardest and how wide the gender gap runs. Numbers like these turn a familiar complaint into measured fact that universities must answer. Policies on leave, deadlines, and evaluation can then be tuned to the real shape of the penalty. For early-career scholars weighing family timing, the study offers a clear view of the costs the current system imposes.
plos-pone-0358183:
Haojie Wang led a team of eight authors studying children with flexible flatfoot, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Kids with this condition often walk in a way that looks normal overall. The team suspected that joints higher up the leg quietly compensate, and set out to check both standing alignment and movement.

Wang's dual-level study found compensatory misalignment near the hip despite the preserved overall gait. Hidden misalignment matters because it loads hips and knees unevenly over a lifetime of walking. Doctors who judge flatfoot by gait alone may miss it. The findings argue for looking at the whole leg in these children, so small corrections now can prevent joint trouble decades later.
plos-pone-0352583:
Puhong Zhang led a team of eight authors trialing a digital tool for sick children in rural China, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rural clinics often lack enough doctors trained in childhood illness. The team tested an electronic platform that guides care, running a cluster randomized trial to check both its accuracy and its efficiency.

Zhang's trial design, randomizing by clinic rather than by child, fits how such tools are really rolled out. The results show whether digital guidance genuinely improves care where it is needed most. Supporters of health technology need trials like this, not pilot enthusiasm. If the platform works, it offers a scalable way to raise care quality across many villages at once.
plos-pone-0356383:
Khawja Imran Masud led a team of six authors building a phone-ready tool for rice disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rice diseases cut harvests, and farmers need diagnosis on the spot, in the field. Their model, IoT-RiceMobileNet, improves a lightweight network design to detect several rice diseases in real time through connected devices.

Masud's model is built to run on modest hardware, bringing a plant doctor to the paddy field. Fast, cheap detection lets farmers treat early and spare healthy crops from blanket spraying. That saves money and reduces chemical use. Lightweight AI that works on the phones farmers already own is more useful than a stronger model that needs a data center.
plos-pone-0357983:
Anna Maria Schneider, Timo Stöver, and Tobias Weissgerber published a 2026 hearing study in PLOS ONE on how seeing a speaker's mouth helps people understand speech in noise. They tested normal-hearing adults and bilateral implant users on a sentence test: sound alone, sight alone, and both together. The visual side came either from video of a real woman speaking or from a computer-animated male avatar, asking whether a virtual face works as well as a real one.

Real-speaker video improved understanding for both groups, and the benefit was larger for implant users, who also proved far better lipreaders than normal-hearing adults. Implant users' lipreading matched their own self-assessments closely. The avatar gave no measurable benefit to anyone. Listening effort barely dropped even when understanding improved. Clinics, they suggest, should add sight-and-sound testing for implant outcomes, using real speakers, not avatars.
plos-pone-0357383:
Caoying Wu and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on melanoma in Xinjiang, China, where the aggressive skin cancer looks different from its Western pattern. Melanoma is far rarer in Asian populations, and more often appears on palms, soles, or mucous membranes than on sun-exposed skin. The team reviewed just over three hundred fifty patients, charting tumor features and following survival and recurrence.

Median survival ran to about six and a half years. Advanced stage and a high level of a blood enzyme, LDH, independently predicted worse survival, Stage, spread, that enzyme, and a comorbidity score predicted recurrence. Extra therapy after surgery protected against it. The drivers differed by subtype: comorbidity burden dominated in cutaneous melanoma, while higher body weight worsened recurrence in the acral form common on hands and feet. The authors press for management that respects subtype rather than importing Western melanoma playbooks wholesale.
plos-pone-0356183:
Jingru Qu, Ling Dai, and Mengjie Yin published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on the questions students ask when they talk philosophy with a large language model. Just over a hundred first-year postgraduates at a Chinese university used a university chatbot for a course assignment. Every student question was coded by thinking level, from recall to evaluation and creation, then students were profiled and their questioning traced across rounds.

Three profiles emerged: students asking mostly for facts, those pressing for explanations, and those pushing toward evaluation. Over time, students split into two paths. One group stalled at applying and analyzing, while the other climbed toward judging and exploring. Fact-focused questioners reported the weakest critical and creative engagement, and the plateauing group reported weaker critical engagement too. For course designers: what students ask predicts engagement depth, so scaffolds should push questioning upward early, before habits lock in.
plos-pone-0357483:
Jiratchaya Puenpa and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE tracking two ordinary coronaviruses, NL63 and OC43, through Thailand in 2024 and 2025. These endemic cousins of the pandemic virus cause everyday respiratory infections, but Southeast Asia had little combined testing and genomic surveillance. The team screened over eleven thousand respiratory specimens, sequenced part of the spike gene from positives, and placed Thai viruses on global family trees.

Positivity ran near four percent in both years, spiking in winter and sagging when the pandemic virus surged. The two viruses differed in make-up: OC43 split evenly between two genotypes, while NL63 was led by one, with two others common. Thai sequences scattered across global diversity, evidence of repeated introductions rather than one local lineage, with movement in both directions across borders. Genetic diversity sagged after 2020, more sharply for OC43, setting a baseline for watching these background viruses.
plos-pone-0351883:
Chongyang Wang and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on soil poisoned by sulfates, solidified with binders made entirely from solid waste. Such ground can fail as water and salt migrate through it, and older models ignored that the binder keeps changing as it hydrates. The team built a migration model tracking hydration over time, using porosity, how open the pore network is, as the master variable. It is linked to soil suction through a fitted curve. Grey correlation analysis describes how reaction products evolve.

Experiments clarified the levers: more binder and more slag tightened the pore structure, while more salt loosened it, and tighter pores slowed water and salt movement. With porosity at its center, the model can forecast how a recipe's defenses change as curing proceeds. The framework is offered as design theory for treating sulfate ground with waste-based materials instead of cement.
plos-pone-0356683:
Elizabeth S Allen and colleagues produced the first large American update of blood group frequencies in two decades. It is also the first to count patients alongside donors. Their 2026 study pooled typing records from five California academic centers and a national blood service. The records covered nearly half a million patients. They covered more than eight million donors across the United States over five years.

Group O dominated everywhere but ran higher among donors than patients. RhD-positive shares also differed. Patient frequencies shifted significantly by hospital, age, and sex. The mismatch matters. Blood banks stock what donors give, but hospitals transfuse what patients need, and the two distributions are not the same. The authors argue recruitment and inventory planning should be tuned to the patient side.
plos-pone-0353983:
Rebecca K Nash, Sangeeta Bhatia, Jack Wardle, Anne Cori, and Pierre Nouvellet solved a practical forecasting problem: epidemic models want daily case counts, but exhausted health systems often report weekly. Their 2026 study built a statistical reconstruction method that unfolds weekly COVID-19 totals back into plausible daily series, then tested epidemic forecasts on data from thirteen American states.

Forecasts fed with reconstructed daily counts performed just as well as forecasts fed the true daily data across the 2020 to 2022 period. That parity matters for the next emergency: when daily reporting becomes unsustainable, or in places that never had it, modelers need not fly blind. Weekly reports, properly unfolded, can carry real-time prediction.
plos-pone-0353483:
Ummehani Mimi, Md Rezaul Karim, Sultana Begum, and Khadiza Akter Eme mapped malaria across Bangladesh's districts with Bayesian disease mapping models, asking where vulnerability truly concentrates as national cases fall. Their 2026 spatial study built district risk from disaster statistics covering 2015 to 2020, national elimination plan data, world malaria reports, and rainfall records, using models that borrow strength from neighboring districts.

The national trend points down, in line with the country's 2030 elimination target. But the maps show stubborn geographic clustering: risk bunches in particular districts rather than fading evenly, and spatial statistics confirm the pattern is real. For an elimination program, the message is to aim the last mile at the map's hotspots.
plos-pone-0351683:
Xianan Miao and colleagues investigate a costly failure in oil wells in this 2026 engineering study from China's Daqing Oilfield. Late in a field's life, heavy water injection can soak a weak rock layer called a marker bed, softening it until the steel casing of nearby wells bends or collapses. The team took one typical damaged well and combined theory, lab tests, and computer simulation to trace how the damage develops.

Their model reproduced the measured narrowing of the real well's casing closely. Damage clustered where the marker bed meets stiffer layers, and the rock grew weaker the longer it soaked. Of the factors tested, injection pressure mattered most, followed by the bed's thickness. Based on a minimum safe casing width, the authors propose pressure limits for different zones to prevent further failures.
plos-pone-0355383:
Gabriel Kwaku Agbeshie and seven colleagues publish a protocol in 2026 for a systematic review on light and children's eyesight. Shortsightedness is rising fast among children worldwide, and early evidence hints that the color mix of everyday light, not just its brightness, may influence how eyes grow. Published studies differ so much in design and measurement that no clear answer has emerged.

Under the registered plan, the team will search eight major databases for human studies and trials linking features of light, such as wavelength and intensity patterns, to changes in children's myopia. Two reviewers will screen and appraise each study independently, and results will be combined where studies are similar enough. The finished review should show which kinds of light look protective and guide trials and lighting policy for schools and homes.
plos-pone-0356283:
Shuang Wu, Yuki Shimizu, and Xiyue Chen study how the face a smile follows changes how we watch it, in this 2026 eye-tracking experiment. Participants viewed short films in which a face melted either from anger or from a neutral expression into a smile, while cameras tracked where their eyes rested. Afterwards they rated how sincere and happy or angry the smiling person seemed.

Judgments of the final smile did not differ between the two conditions, but looking behavior did: after anger, viewers spent longer on the eyes. Across both conditions, more time spent looking at the mouth went with kinder judgments, seeing the smile as more sincere and happy and less angry. Gaze also drifted over time from the nose toward the eyes and mouth. The authors suggest attention to the mouth may soften the residue of a prior angry expression.
plos-pone-0356483:
Maria Grazia Santi and five colleagues, with a collaborating group, test whether artificial intelligence can capture a prosthetist's hands-on judgment, in this 2026 proof-of-concept study. The socket of an above-knee prosthesis must be reshaped, or rectified, to fit a residual limb, and that reshaping depends heavily on individual craft skill. Working with nine patients of a single prosthetist, the team scanned limbs before and after manual rectification and trained an algorithm on the differences.

The system distilled the prosthetist's habits into an average template plus a few main patterns of variation, capturing both stated rules and tacit moves. In leave-one-out testing, AI-shaped models differed from the hand-made ones by volumes within clinically acceptable limits for every patient. The authors suggest such templates could support training, documentation, and care in places short of expert prosthetists.
plos-pone-0355483:
Getaneh Atikilt Yemata and colleagues followed hospital records of Ethiopian patients with high blood pressure to track kidney decline. High blood pressure drives chronic kidney disease, yet local data on how fast kidneys fail were scarce. Their 2026 study reviewed five years of records from hospitals in the South Gondar Zone.

Progression to kidney disease appeared at a median of just under four years of follow-up. The rate was roughly nine to ten new cases per thousand patient-months. Uncontrolled blood pressure, obesity, and high blood fats each sped progression clearly. Yemata and colleagues argue that tighter pressure control and weight care in routine hypertension clinics could slow kidney loss in the region.
plos-pone-0354883:
Caecilia Doorenbos and colleagues run in 2026 a small blinded pilot on adding creatine, a muscle energy compound, directly into dialysis fluid for kidney patients. Dialysis patients often run low on creatine, which links to worse life quality and survival. Groups received rising doses in the fluid over six weeks, with some receiving a dummy fluid instead.

Treatment was mostly well tolerated, with no serious harmful events and one dropout tied to a possible side effect. Creatine levels in red cells and blood plasma rose with dose compared with dummy treatment. The pilot supports a larger trial to test whether raising levels improves health.
plos-pone-0354083:
Catiana L Engelhardt and three colleagues published this 2026 randomized trial of positive psychotherapy for anxiety disorders delivered in online groups. One hundred and six participants received either full therapist support across ten long weekly sessions, or minimal support: three short sessions plus videos for the remaining weeks.

Both formats improved anxiety, and the lightly supported version held up surprisingly well against the full one. Engelhardt notes the participants were mostly women, so wider samples are needed. The findings challenge assumptions that constant therapist contact is essential, and hint at cheaper group care.
plos-pone-0353883:
Diego Silva Figueiredo and three colleagues published this 2026 chart study of myasthenia gravis care at a Brazilian public hospital. One hundred and fifty adults treated in 2024 and 2025 had their symptoms, immune markers, treatments, and path to diagnosis reconstructed from records and questionnaires. They were then grouped by how well drugs controlled the disease.

Patient profiles matched international reports, but diagnosis often came late, and many patients depended on steroids or resisted standard drugs. Figueiredo urges earlier recognition, better and earlier access to specialist care, and steroid-sparing strategies in public systems.
plos-pone-0352983:
Mutesi Magololo and colleagues, in a 2026 study, audit antibiotic use on the surgical wards of Uganda's national referral hospital. Wrong use of antibiotics in surgery feeds drug resistance, a growing threat where lab support is thin. The team counted prescriptions on set survey days, reviewed lab records of resistance, and interviewed health workers.

Nearly two thirds of about three hundred surgical patients were on at least one antibiotic. Almost all prescriptions were preventive doses meant to guard the surgical wound, yet nearly all of those ran past the first day, far longer than guidelines advise. Two broad drugs dominated the list. More than half of the prescriptions came from the global Watch group, drugs meant to be used with extra care. Staff knew stewardship principles, but formal systems to police prescribing were patchy, and slow lab results pushed doctors to prescribe blind. The team calls for working stewardship teams.
plos-pone-0354583:
Lyu and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a leaner vision model that spots tea leaf diseases in real time. Diseased leaves cut tea quality and yield, but the best detection models are too heavy for the small computers farms can run in the field. Their design trims a popular detection model and adds a trick that sharpens its sense of where things are.

The trimmed model sheds about a third of its parts and a quarter of its computing work. It also gains an attention step that weighs the position of features, helping it catch faint disease marks. On test images it scored near the top for detection accuracy, beating the untrimmed starting model. The team plugged it into a working service that writes reports on its own and runs on ordinary processors. They present it as proof that accurate crop checks can run on cheap hardware.
plos-pone-0354383:
Akter and colleagues, in a 2026 computer study, hunt for a molecule that could jam a key toxin of Helicobacter pylori, the stomach bacterium behind gastritis, ulcers, and some stomach cancers. Antibiotics against it are losing ground to resistance. The toxin, VacA, helps the bacterium damage stomach cells, and every strain carries it.

Starting from a database of thousands of drug-like molecules, docking software fitted each into the toxin's active pocket. Only a fraction bound at all, and screening for safety and drug-like traits left one winner, identified by its database code. A long motion simulation showed the winner settled stably against the toxin, with steady bonds and favorable energy. The authors are explicit that this is an in silico hit, a candidate born on a computer. Wet-lab tests must now show whether it truly blocks the toxin.
plos-pone-0353783:
Ezzi and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a hospital study in Metz, France, on how strictly to isolate patients carrying drug-resistant gut bacteria. These bacteria shrug off key antibiotics and spread in hospitals, especially on wards for older patients, who often carry them. Full contact precautions for every carrier are costly and burdensome, and their benefit in such wards has been questioned.

Two geriatric departments will alternate in blocks between two strategies: precautions for all known carriers, and standard care with precautions only when clinical signs trigger them. Which ward starts with which strategy is assigned at random. Spread of the bacteria will be tracked under both regimes to test whether the lighter approach is not worse. As a protocol, the paper fixes the design and reasoning in advance; whether hospitals can safely relax isolation on geriatric wards will be answered by the results.
plos-pone-0353283:
Amélia Fernandes Nunes and four colleagues examine short-sightedness in Portuguese teenagers, asking how much parents and school life each contribute, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Eight hundred and seventy-four adolescents aged ten to eighteen had their eyes measured and answered, with their parents, questions about outdoor time, screens, sport, and study load. About twenty-two percent were myopic by the study's definition.

A parent's myopia was by far the strongest association, with odds rising toward fourfold. Being further along in school and attending an urban school added risk too. In a low-density region the rate matched denser parts of Europe, suggesting school-centred habits travel with the school system itself. Outdoor time remains the authors' practical lever.
plos-pone-0353383:
Christiane Barthel and six colleagues ask a practical question. Do wrist fractures fixed at night fare worse than those fixed in office hours? Their study came from one hospital. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Six hundred and sixty patients had a broken wrist set with a metal plate. The cases spanned nine years. Patients were split by surgery time. Then they were matched carefully. Fracture type, age, and sex were balanced into two equal groups.

Every outcome was compared across the groups. Operating time matched. Bone realignment on X-ray matched. Complications and later wrist movement matched too. The authors are careful about the claim. No difference in one hospital is not proof of equality everywhere. But within this service, the night team carried no measurable penalty.
plos-pone-0353683:
Gholampour and colleagues built a computer aid for planning where stroke patients go after hospital care in a 2026 study. Going home, going home with help, moving to special care, or dying in hospital each call for different planning. The team used routine records for more than seventeen hundred patients with stroke or a brief mini-stroke.

Ten prediction methods were tested, and a neural network performed best overall, though its accuracy stayed moderate. The system also names the record items that push a prediction up or down, so staff can see why a result appears. That openness matters in care settings, where a score alone is not enough for families and teams to trust a plan.
plos-pone-0352783:
Corbett and colleagues interviewed workers who had faced sexual harassment on the job in a 2026 study. Thirty workers, mostly from service jobs around San Francisco, described what employers did and what they wished employers had done. Their views center the targets of harassment rather than company policy papers.

Workers asked for two things above all: clear rules that harassment will not be tolerated, and real responses when it happens. Helpful responses included an independent reporting channel, spoken support, and action that protected the target. The findings give managers a target's-eye checklist for prevention and response that goes beyond legal minimums.
plos-pone-0352283:
Benkhelfa and colleagues surveyed primary schools across Greater London on children's activity in a 2026 study. A survey built on World Health Organization guidance went to every state primary school in the capital's boroughs. About one school in ten replied, with at least one from every borough.

Most replying schools reported policies matching the global whole-school approach, covering lessons, breaks, travel, and after-school options. Still, the authors found weak spots inside several areas, and warn that having policies on paper may not raise children's actual activity. The survey sets a baseline for testing whether school activity plans change behavior, especially in poorer neighborhoods.
plos-pone-0353183:
Swarna and colleagues estimated face and jaw injuries in Bangladesh from a national survey in a 2026 study. The survey covered nearly three hundred thousand people with a six-month recall window, giving the first population-level picture for the country. Annual rates were worked out overall and by age, sex, and care patterns.

Non-fatal face injuries struck at a rate of several hundred per hundred thousand people each year by their estimate. The study also weighed health system load and household costs. Face injuries can impair eating, speech, and appearance, so their burden runs deeper than counts suggest. National numbers give planners a basis for prevention and trauma care funding.
plos-pone-0352683:
Bum-Kyu Kim and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One paper on recognizing ships from underwater sound recordings when only a few examples are available. Navies and researchers often cannot gather large labeled collections for every vessel type, especially where security limits access. The authors build a learning system that can tell ship types apart from just a handful of sample signals.

Their model compares a new recording against stored examples and also weighs how much signals vary within and between ship types. It reached strong accuracy at picking the right class among five options and could handle ship types it had never been trained on. That flexibility matters for ocean monitoring, where new vessels appear and labeled data stay scarce.
plos-pone-0351983:
Hiroshi Imamura and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One methods study on formulas used to estimate a healthy liver's standard volume, a number surgeons need when planning transplants and liver removal. Many competing formulas exist, and past checks often tested them on age groups far outside the ones used to build them. The team re-tested thirteen formulas, each only within its original age range, against CT-measured liver volumes.

In more than eleven hundred people without liver disease, two formulas matched measured volumes best when kept inside their intended ages. Used beyond those ages, the formulas drifted because livers themselves shrink with age after about fifty. The study offers surgeons a cleaner way to judge which formula to trust, and a general lesson on testing prediction tools fairly.
plos-pone-0332983:
Zahra Jahanbakhti and Zahra Momeni present this 2026 PLOS One dental study from Karaj, Iran. It covers orphaned children aged six to twelve in four state-run centers. The team asked the children about oral health knowledge, attitudes, and habits. Then they examined teeth, gums, and cleanliness with standard clinical tools.

Knowledge scores were low. Fewer than a third of baby molars were fully sound. More than half of the first permanent molars already showed early decay. Hygiene overall was fair, and gum inflammation was mild. Frequent brushing predicted better oral status. So did more positive attitudes. Knowledge alone did not. The authors recommend teaching aimed at caregivers. They also recommend routine dental checks for this vulnerable group.
plos-pone-0352183:
Young-Gwan Kim, Do-Hyeon Ryu, and Kwang-Jae Kim ask why smart home automation spreads so slowly in South Korea. Their 2026 study surveyed one hundred sixty-seven people who do not yet use such systems. Two personal factors took centre stage. One is lifestyle: how a household actually lives. The other is how difficult automation feels to set up and use. The authors folded both into the standard technology acceptance model and tested the result.

Lifestyle cut both ways. An energy-saving lifestyle surprisingly lowered intention to adopt. Households short on time for chores, meanwhile, wanted automation more. Perceived difficulty hurt twice over. Struggling with configuration made the technology seem less useful and less desirable. Companies therefore face two different sales problems. Busy households need only a nudge. Confident energy-savers need a different pitch entirely, and everyone needs painless setup before clever features matter.
plos-pone-0350983:
Wenping Luo, Xiao Wei, and Qian Xiao trace how low blood sugar injures heart arteries in diabetes. Their 2026 study combines a diabetic mouse model with cultured vessel-lining cells cycled between low and high glucose. Hypoglycemia raises the risk of coronary events sharply. The mechanism hunted here involves nitric oxide, a vessel signal, and an innate immune alarm pathway called cGAS-STING. Genetic knockouts and inhibitors let the team order the chain of events.

Hypoglycemia roughly quadrupled nitric oxide in the vessel cells. Their mitochondria faltered, producing about half the usual energy. Blocking the enzyme making the excess nitric oxide reversed much damage. Mitochondrial DNA leaked out at nearly six times the normal rate. That leaked DNA appears to trip the immune alarm. Removing the alarm's STING component silenced the pathway but not the leak. The chain matters: it names drug targets for protecting diabetic hearts from sugar crashes.
plos-pone-0352383:
Mesheil Alalyani and seven colleagues test whether burnout bridges hospital culture and nurses leaving. Their 2026 cross-sectional study surveys three hundred fifty-five nurses in Saudi Arabia. Five Ministry of Health hospitals in two regions took part. Nurses were sampled proportionally from a population of twenty-five hundred. Questionnaires measured workplace culture, burnout, and intention to stay. The analysis follows the Job Demands-Resources model, a standard frame for how workplaces exhaust or sustain staff.

Culture and burnout have each been tied to turnover before. Nobody in the Saudi context had tested the chain reaction, though. Does a poor culture burn nurses out? And is that burnout what loosens their intention to stay? Mediation analysis answers that. The distinction matters practically. If burnout carries the effect, managers must fix workload and recovery, not just polish culture statements. Retention money follows the mechanism, and this study is built to name it.
plos-pone-0348383:
Sickle cell disease strains the heart over time, yet heart ultrasound data from Latin America are scarce. Martin E Arrieta-Mendoza and colleagues profiled adults with the disease at a major hospital in Cali, Colombia, in this 2026 PLOS One record review covering 2022 to 2024.

Fifty-seven patients qualified from hundreds screened. Most were in their twenties, and about two thirds took hydroxyurea, a standard protective drug. The team recorded heart size, pumping and filling function, and pressure measures, alongside blood values. Their aim was to spot which ultrasound signs travel with higher cardiovascular risk in this population, guiding closer follow-up for those who need it.
plos-pone-0351183:
Respiratory syncytial virus sends many Canadian babies to hospital each winter, and new long-acting antibody shots plus a pregnancy vaccine have widened prevention choices. Gebremedhin B Gebretekle and colleagues compared seven seasonal programs for cost and health gain, in this 2026 PLOS One analysis.

Their model weighed health system and wider social costs against years of healthy life, using a standard value threshold. A combined approach came out best: vaccinate mothers due during virus season, and give antibody shots to other infants. Rankings shifted with product prices, the authors note, so the cheapest sensible program depends on deals governments strike with makers.
plos-pone-0344883:
Nguyen Huy Hoang Vu and Bao Long Nguyen ran a large statistical sweep on seventy eight thousand proteins to find which sequence traits separate proteins that dissolve well from those that clump. Dissolving matters for making proteins in labs and factories. Thirty six chemical traits were compared with strict error control, effect sizes, and accuracy curves.

Nearly all traits differed significantly, yet most effects were tiny with heavy overlap. Size traits led, and a share of negative charge helped modestly. Size measures duplicated each other almost perfectly. A lean score joining length and negative charge did best, but accuracy stayed modest. Dissolving is governed by many weak pushes, not one master trait.
plos-pone-0349583:
Mariana Carvalho Sturaro, Ruana Carolina Cabral da Silva, and Simone Simionatto studied how pairing two antibiotics changes gene activity in a highly drug resistant Klebsiella germ that causes hospital infections. Computer analysis mapped six wall building and resistance genes, then cultures dosed with each drug alone and paired were read for gene activity at two and four hours.

Gene maps placed resistance tools in the germs outer skins and wall control genes in its inner membrane, matching known biology. Paired dosing shifted wall and resistance gene activity in ways single drugs did not, hinting at why the pair kills better together. Understanding pair mechanics helps revive old antibiotics against germs that defeat them singly.
plos-pone-0349683:
Raju Rana and co-authors studied insulin resistance scores and vitamin D in adults with metabolic syndrome in 2026. Low vitamin D and the syndrome travel together worldwide, and cheap combined scores might flag who is lowest.

Nearly thirteen hundred adults at health checkups were split by a triglyceride glucose score and its body mass variant. The body mass combined score showed a weak but real negative link with vitamin D levels, while the plain score showed none. Blood fats and sugar differed across score bands, and men scored higher on the index. The weak size of the link tempers any screening hopes.
plos-pone-0350383:
Katharine Holmes and Lindsay Bottoms mapped research on fencing and wheelchair fencing in 2026. Both sports are growing and attracting science, but the shape of that science, its methods and themes, had never been charted.

Three databases were searched for experimental and measured observational studies of fencers. Four hundred forty-five studies qualified. Output jumped after 2015. Laboratory and snapshot designs dominated, while long term follow-ups and randomised trials were rare. The map shows a young field strong on measurement and short on intervention proof, a clear agenda for the next decade of fencing research funding.
plos-pone-0323983:
Hannock Tweya and colleagues traced how people starting HIV treatment in Lilongwe, Malawi, stayed connected to care over their first two years. Staying on antiretroviral therapy keeps people healthy and lowers spread of the virus. Clinics there support new patients either with a peer helper called a Buddy or with a two-way texting service for those with phones. Their 2026 study covered more than six thousand clients at two public clinics.

Texting clients stayed most consistently engaged through the first eighteen months, and about seven in ten were still in care at two years. Buddy clients without phones fared worst, with only about a quarter retained. Many who stayed had gaps, arriving late or returning after long absences. The authors argue support should adapt to each person's pattern of attendance over time.
plos-pone-0349883:
Ghulam Shere Raza, Marjo-Riitta Järvelin, and co-authors measured a liver protein in the blood of people from three age groups to see what drives its level. Exercise releases this protein, called GPLD1, in mice, where it supports new brain cell growth and better memory. Human evidence was scarce. Their 2026 study compared young exercising adults, older adults, and middle-aged adults with prediabetes.

The prediabetic group carried the highest protein levels, and older adults with diabetes had more than those without. In older adults, more daily steps seemed linked to lower levels until diabetes was accounted for, which explained the pattern away. Moderate exercise in the young changed nothing. The authors conclude that age and diabetes shape blood levels of the protein, and its role in human thinking still needs direct study.
plos-pone-0350083:
Supachai Trikisayaveach and co-authors studied a common danger for kidney failure patients at the start of surgery: a sharp drop in blood pressure after anesthesia begins. These patients are prone to unstable circulation, yet evidence specific to them was limited. Their 2026 review covered more than six hundred adults with end-stage kidney disease who had non-heart surgery under general anesthesia over a decade.

Nearly forty-four in every hundred patients developed the pressure drop within twenty minutes of induction. Five factors raised the odds: age over sixty-five, long-term use of oral diabetes medicines, a higher dose of the induction drug propofol, rapid-sequence induction, and emergency surgery. Dialysis-related details, by contrast, showed no clear link. The authors say knowing these predictors can help anesthesia teams prepare support before the pressure falls.
plos-pone-0350183:
Xinjuan Zhou and co-authors evaluated a Chinese insurance reform that began pooling outpatient costs for employees, using survey data from middle-aged adults. The reform aimed to make clinic visits more affordable for workers aged forty-five to sixty. Their 2026 analysis of a national aging survey's 2018 wave, from the pilot period, modeled who visited clinics, how often, and what they paid themselves.

Where pooling operated, the chance of an outpatient visit rose by about five percentage points and visit frequency climbed substantially. Strikingly, expected out-of-pocket spending was also higher in policy regions, by roughly half. Richer benefit levels drew stronger responses, and people with several chronic conditions used more care. The authors say the pilot's behavior patterns remain relevant to the national scheme that followed.
plos-pone-0343183:
Clement Torrent, Melania Capasso, and co-authors fed aging mice low-dose rapamycin, a transplant drug that extends lifespan in many species, to see exactly which immune changes it causes in old age. Worry persists that a proven immune suppressant is a risky anti-aging bet. Their 2026 study profiled immune cells across tissues after long treatment, then challenged the animals with a bacterial trigger of inflammation.

Most immune populations, including the brain's resident microglia, barely changed. What did shrink was the age-related buildup of a specific T cell type that produces an inflammatory signal, especially around the abdomen. After the challenge, that signal ran lower in treated animals and their brain immune cells stayed calmer. The authors describe a narrow, targeted effect rather than broad suppression.
plos-pone-0350283:
Tewodros Denekew Haile and co-authors bought ciprofloxacin antibiotic tablets from shops across Ethiopia's West Gondar Zone and tested how fast each brand dissolves, a stand-in for how the body absorbs it. Tablets that dissolve too slowly or unevenly may fail patients, and local data on brand quality were scarce. Their 2026 study collected twenty samples from six towns using mystery shoppers, then ran standard laboratory dissolution tests at the national drug authority.

Brands differed in how quickly the drug was released, and mathematical models of the release curves pointed to different underlying mechanisms between products. Some comparisons fell outside the similarity bounds regulators use to call brands interchangeable. The authors argue the findings justify tighter market surveillance, since a familiar name on the box does not guarantee equivalent performance.
plos-pone-0349383:
Peter Pany and colleagues built a new tool to measure how much attention people pay to plants in a busy natural scene, a blind spot known as plant awareness disparity. Their instrument hides objects inside a rich landscape picture and combines the search with eye tracking, recall tests, and species naming. Three sub-studies developed and checked the picture and the method.

Eye tracking showed that how big an object is, or how long eyes rest on it, did not predict whether people remembered it. Experts recalled plants with high prominence and named them precisely, while students used broad words like tree or field. A validated measure like this lets educators test whether teaching actually sharpens attention to plants.
plos-pone-0347783:
Touria Essayagh and colleagues surveyed more than eighteen hundred Moroccan schoolgirls aged eleven to fourteen about the vaccine against human papillomavirus, which prevents most cervical cancer. Face-to-face interviews across the country in spring 2025 measured what the girls knew and how hesitant they and their families felt. Hesitancy turned out to be overwhelming.

Nearly nine in ten girls were classified as hesitant. The strongest driver was having unvaccinated peers, followed by a father who could not read, weak recommendation from health workers, and the belief that the vaccine encourages sexual activity. Each factor is a lever: strong advice from trusted health staff and better parent information directly address the largest risks the study found.
plos-pone-0348883:
Chao Hong and colleagues built an optimization model for scheduling shared passenger drones across a multi-airport city network. Riders book trips with origins, destinations, group sizes, preferred craft, and arrival times, while each drone has a position, battery range, seats, and speed. Matching the two sides in real time, without making passengers wait or miss badly, is a hard puzzle.

Their solver, a self-learning variant of the ant-lion algorithm, tracks seats as it assigns routes and allows soft arrival windows, so small delays cost less than large ones. Simulations cut total system travel time substantially against benchmarks. Urban air taxis will live or die on dispatch quality, and this model treats passenger comfort and fleet efficiency together.
plos-pone-0348683:
Johan Azañero-Haro and Alonso Soto raced four scoring systems that predict death in hospitalised COVID-19 pneumonia against each other using Peruvian patients from the first pandemic wave. All the patients were unvaccinated, and just over a thousand had complete data for every score. The scores blend bedside observations and lab values into a single risk number meant to guide scarce care.

The quickest score, built from breathing rate, oxygen level, and consciousness, separated survivors from those who died better than the three rivals, including the large international benchmark. The weakest score lagged well behind. Checking how the groups compared also showed the analysed patients fairly represented the whole cohort. The authors recommend the winning score for busy hospitals, while noting calibration quirks that local teams should watch.
plos-pone-0348783:
Othman Eldalal and colleagues produced the first deep protein portrait of lab-grown neutrophil stand-ins made with a less common recipe. Researchers grow HL-60 leukaemia cells into neutrophil-like cells to study these frontline immune cells safely. The classic recipe uses one solvent and the alternative another. Nobody had compared their protein contents in depth. The team measured growth, surface markers, germ-killing chemistry, and thousands of proteins in both versions.

Both recipes made convincing neutrophil-like cells, but the alternative kept cells dividing faster and scored lower on one maturity marker, while its protein mix highlighted granule release and oxidant pathways. A stress-sensing protein family stood out in the alternative version. The authors give labs a molecular map for choosing which recipe suits the question at hand.
plos-pone-0337883:
Nadine Schrode and co-workers catalog the immune cells living in human breast milk, one cell at a time. Milk carries a mother's white blood cells that help guard and shape a baby's defenses. Their 2026 study reads gene activity in more than twenty-three thousand milk cells from nine healthy donors, hunting for cell types earlier work had missed.

Eighteen distinct groups appeared, most of them scavenger and messenger cells of the immune system. Two odd groups mixed skin-like and immune traits. Many cells showed signs of adapting to milk's fatty setting, handling fats and presenting germ clues to other cells. Each mother also had her own mix, with some groups found in only one or two donors.
plos-pone-0346583:
Max Wiedemann, Christopher Mai, Luca Eisentraut, and Ricardo Buettner built an image-reading system that estimates how much cotton a fabric contains. Knowing fibre content is essential for recycling old textiles, but checking by hand is slow and laboratory spectroscopy is costly. Their 2026 system instead learns from ordinary camera photographs, merging two neural network designs, one good at fine detail and one at overall pattern.

Tested with repeated cross-checks on a reviewed dataset, the model estimated cotton content with an average error of about fourteen percent, the best result yet for a camera-based approach. The authors argue such cheap visual sorting could make textile recycling pay, cutting manual work at sorting plants.
plos-pone-0348283:
Dawit Errega and colleagues gathered everything published on heart and blood vessel disease among Ethiopians living with HIV. People with HIV face extra cardiovascular risk from the virus itself and from some of its medicines, yet Ethiopian evidence had never been pulled together. Their 2026 scoping review, searching six databases, found twenty-six studies.

Nearly two-thirds of the research concerned high blood pressure alone, which affected between eleven and forty-one percent of patients depending on the study. Smoking, alcohol, older age, weight, and long treatment histories recurred as risk factors. Other conditions, from stroke to heart muscle disease, were barely studied. The authors call for broader, stronger, community-based research.
plos-pone-0345383:
Ivan P. Gorlov, Olga Y. Gorlova, and Aaron P. Thrift asked whether differences in liver gene activity help explain why fatty liver disease strikes Black and White Americans at different rates. They analysed gene expression from liver biopsies of more than three hundred people who had weight-loss surgery, comparing samples across stages from healthy liver to advanced inflamed disease.

Over two hundred genes behaved differently between the groups, and genes driving disease progression were over-represented among them. Each group carried its own candidate drivers, and the expression gap widened as disease advanced. The authors argue that biology inside the liver, not only lifestyle and income, shapes the racial disparity, with implications for targeted prevention.
plos-pone-0348583:
Jemil Yasin Shifa and Abrham Seyoum Tsehay asked if climate-wise farm work lifts poor homes in more ways than cash. They spoke with four hundred sixteen small farms in the Siltie Zone of Ethiopia. Their gauge of want spanned health, school, and home needs. They also used care in the sums, to guard against rich farms just taking up more new ways.

Take-up of climate-wise work cut want in a clear way. More take-up brought more gain. The team reads this as proof that such work does two jobs at once. It shields farms from harsh skies and eases daily want. They urge aid aimed at the poorest homes.
plos-pone-0348083:
Shuang Deng and Zhongqiang Guo hunt for tipping points in blood fats and frailty. Their study of older adults appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The data came from a large Chinese aging survey. It held close to three thousand people. Several hundred had severe limits on airflow, a late stage of lung disease.

Two measures stood out from the rest. One fat-based index tied to lower odds of severe limits overall. Leftover cholesterol in the blood showed a sharp threshold. Below that line, its tie was very strong. Above it, the tie faded but stayed real. Age, sex, and schooling shifted some links. Such cut points could help doctors set precise goals.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Macedonia, newly independent from Yugoslavia, feared the wars around it might spill across its borders. The UN force already watching its frontier was given a new name and identity by Resolution 983, adopted unanimously on 31 March 1995, following the Secretary-General's report of 22 March.

The troops serving with the protection force in Macedonia became UNPREDEP, the UN Preventive Deployment Force, a mission notable for deploying before a conflict starts rather than after. Its mandate was set to run until 30 November 1995. The Council urged cooperation with European security observers and asked member states to support the force's needs.

North Korea's tanks rolled south on 25 June 1950. The Council had ruled the attack a breach of the peace. It told the North to halt and pull back to the 38th parallel. The North did not obey. Word came that its troops fought on. Resolution 83 passed on 27 June 1950 by seven votes to one. Yugoslavia said no. The Soviet team was away, in boycott.

The Council urged all member states to help South Korea. Aid could flow in what shape the fight required. The aim was to beat back the attack. Peace and safety in the area had to be restored. Seoul's plea for swift help was cited in the text. Two states, Egypt and India, sat the vote out. The plea built the legal base for the US-led war under the UN flag.

Resolution 1583, adopted unanimously on 28 January 2005, extends the UN force in southern Lebanon for six more months. UNIFIL had patrolled since 1978, but its job had changed: the Secretary-General had confirmed that Israel completed its withdrawal from Lebanon in June 2000, as an earlier landmark resolution required. What remained was restoring calm along the Blue Line, where tension and violence persisted.

Answering Lebanon's request, the Council renewed the force's mandate for a further six-month period. It repeated that UNIFIL was an interim arrangement, not a permanent fixture. The text also echoed earlier calls on peacekeeper safety and on training personnel to prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS and other diseases in UN operations.

Resolution 1683, passed on 13 June 2006, opens two small gaps in Liberia's arms ban. The ban dated from 2003, when guns fed the war. By 2006 a new elected chief, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, led the state. Her guards and her new police and troops needed arms to train with. Yet the ban blocked even those. The Council said vetted state forces must take on more of the guard work at home.

The ban would not touch guns and rounds sent in the past for the guard unit's training. Those could stay in its hands for real use. Small lots for other new, vetted units could pass too. Each lot needed the bans team's prior nod, case by case.

Resolution 283, adopted on 29 July 1970 by thirteen votes to none with France and Britain abstaining, tightens the legal isolation of South Africa's rule in Namibia. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and the Council had since declared Pretoria's continued presence illegal. South Africa nonetheless kept enforcing its laws and courts in the territory as if nothing had changed.

The Council reaffirmed that everything South Africa did for or about Namibia after the mandate ended was illegal and invalid. It pointed to the arms embargo on South Africa agreed the week before as part of the pressure. And it pressed states to deal with Namibia only through the United Nations, denying Pretoria the recognition it craved.

Resolution 383, passed on 13 December 1975, keeps the UN force in Cyprus for six more months. A UN report of 8 December judged the force still key, to hold the truce and to aid the hunt for a peace pact. The best path, the report held, was talks between the two groups' men. Such talks could bear fruit if the men came primed and cleared to strike real deals on all the hard points of the Cyprus row.

Both sides backed the plan the report urged, and Cyprus agreed the force should stay past 15 December. Its term thus ran to June 1976. The text cites a November Assembly call as well. That call pressed for swift work on past pledges: troops out, and the displaced back home.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1883 (XVIII), adopted on 14 October 1963, warned against handing power to the sitting government of Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly noted that that government rested on an unfair constitution most people opposed. It noted that giving it control of armed forces would make a tense situation worse.

Britain was invited not to pass any powers or marks of sovereignty to the colony as then governed. It was invited to wait for a government speaking for all the people. The text also asked Britain not to send armed forces and aircraft to the colony. It asked Britain to carry out the earlier Assembly resolutions on the question.

Resolution 69/83, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, covers cooperation between the United Nations and the Council of Europe. It calls for reinforced joint work on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It recognizes the European Court of Human Rights as the key guarantor for the Council's 47 member states. It lists shared fields, from torture prevention, trafficking and children's rights to data protection, cybercrime and anti-corruption work.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Afghan groups had signed the Bonn Agreement the day before, and on 6 December 2001 the Council endorsed it. The deal set up temporary arrangements after the fall of the Taliban, to hold until permanent institutions could be rebuilt. An Interim Authority was due to take office on 22 December.

All Afghan groups are called on to carry out the agreement in full and work with the Interim Authority. The United Nations role in supporting the process is backed. Groups are also pressed to let aid reach people in need, protect aid workers, and respect human rights, while donors are asked to fund relief and rebuilding.

Iraq after the fall of its government in war is the subject of this framework text of 22 May 2003. Iraqis, the Council stresses, must govern themselves soon and control their own resources. The United Nations is cast in a vital role in relief, rebuilding, and restoring representative institutions.

Acting after the invasion, the Council lifted the trade and financial sanctions imposed since 1990, except for the arms embargo. It recognized the occupying powers' joint administration, called the Authority, and urged it to restore security and conditions for self-rule. A Development Fund for Iraq would hold oil revenues under world oversight, and a Special Representative would lead the United Nations work in the country.

Two rounds of talks between Morocco and the POLISARIO Front had been held since June 2007. They were the first face-to-face meetings in years. On 31 October 2007 MINURSO is renewed in Western Sahara, with backing for the new negotiations. Both sides' April proposals remained on the table.

The parties are called on to keep showing political will and to continue negotiating in good faith toward a mutually acceptable solution providing for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. The mission's mandate is renewed alongside the talks. The Secretary-General is to report on the negotiations by 31 January 2008 and on the wider situation before the mandate period ends, and states are asked to fund family-visit measures.

Portugal's African territories return to the agenda on 11 December 1963, after talks failed. The Secretary-General had opened contact between Portugal and African states, but no agreement was reached on what self-determination means. That failure is regretted, as is Lisbon's refusal to follow the July resolution on the territories.

The meaning of self-determination from the General Assembly's 1960 declaration is restated: all peoples may freely choose their political status and pursue their own development. Portugal's non-compliance is deprecated, and all states are called on to honour the arms measures of the earlier text, which barred help for repression. The Secretary-General is to keep working on the question and report by 1 June 1964.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for twelve months on 7 August 2009. Iraq's government was praised for work on democracy, the rule of law, and public order against terrorism and sectarian violence. Security gains were real but fragile, and they had to be locked in by political progress and national reconciliation.

The mandate set in 2007 and 2008 is kept. The mission's head is to advise Iraq on dialogue, elections, constitutional review, internal boundaries, and regional engagement, and to support aid, refugee returns, and human rights. The Secretary-General is to report every three months. Member states are again called on to give the mission the staff, funding, and security support its wider role requires.
un-sc-res-983:
The Macedonia mission gained a new name and shape in March 1995. On 31 March 1995 the Security Council turned UNPROFOR's force there into UNPREDEP. The letters stand for United Nations Preventive Deployment Force. The Secretary-General's report of 22 March supplied the plan. The Council approved the arrangements he set out. The mission's job was to watch borders and deter trouble before it started.

The Council restated its support for Macedonia's independence and borders. It worried about events that could shake the young state's stability. The force would keep working with the European security mission in the country. Member states were asked to help it do its work. It was the United Nations' first preventive deployment.
un-sc-res-83:
North Korea had ignored the order to pull back to the 38th parallel. Fighting in Korea raged on at the end of June 1950. On 27 June 1950 the Security Council found that urgent military measures were needed. North Korea had neither stopped fighting nor withdrawn. United Nations reports from Korea confirmed the defiance. The Council now moved from words to collective action.

It recommends that member states give South Korea the help needed to repel the attack. The goal was to restore peace and security in the area. The vote was seven to one, with Yugoslavia against. Two members did not take part, and the Soviet Union was absent. The text supplied the legal base for the United Nations Command in Korea.
un-sc-res-1583:
Lebanon's United Nations force was renewed by the Security Council on 28 January 2005. Tension and violence persisted along the Blue Line, the withdrawal line confirmed after Israel's pullout in 2000. Lebanon's government had asked on 11 January for six more months of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, UNIFIL. The Secretary-General's report of 20 January noted the risk of escalation.

The Council endorsed that report and extended UNIFIL's mandate to 31 July 2005. It restated its strong support for Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The Lebanese government was called to extend its sole authority through the south, including by deploying its armed forces there. All parties had to give UNIFIL full freedom of movement and respect the Blue Line in its entirety. The Council condemned all acts of violence, including recent fire across the line that had killed and wounded United Nations staff.
un-sc-res-1683:
Liberia's own security forces gained narrow arms exemptions on 13 June 2006. The Council welcomed the leadership of the newly elected president, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, and her work to restore peace and harmony. Newly vetted Liberian forces needed to take over more security work. The arms embargo of resolution 1521 (2003) blocked their supply.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ruled that the embargo would not cover weapons already given to the Special Security Service for training with the sanctions committee's advance approval. Those arms could stay with the service for full operational use. Small supplies for vetted, trained police and security staff could also pass, case by case, with the committee's prior consent. Each grant needed a joint request from Liberia and the exporting state. Liberia then had to mark and register the weapons.
un-sc-res-283:
Namibia's isolation from South Africa was spelled out on 29 July 1970. The mandate had been ended by the General Assembly, and resolutions 264 (1969) and 276 (1970) declared South Africa's presence illegal. Pretoria still refused to withdraw its administration. Its courts and laws ran on in the territory against the territory's international status.

The Council asked all states to cut every tie with South Africa that implied recognition of its authority over Namibia. States with missions in South Africa had to declare formally that they did not recognize that authority. Consular posts covering Namibia were to be closed. State-owned companies had to halt all dealings and new investment in the territory. Governments were told to withhold loans and credits from firms working there and to discourage their nationals from investing in Namibia. The package aimed to starve the occupation of money and legitimacy at once.
un-sc-res-383:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was kept on during a hard winter on 13 December 1975. The Secretary-General's report of 8 December held that the force was still needed to hold the cease-fire. Talks between the two communities offered the best path, he said, but only if the negotiators came ready to bargain on every core issue. Both parties had agreed to six more months.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964) and its texts 365 (1974) and 367 (1975). It called for their urgent and effective application. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint and to speed their cooperative work toward a settlement. The stationing of the force in Cyprus was extended for six months, to 15 June 1976. All parties were asked again to give the force their full cooperation. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and report on the talks.
europmc-pmc10000783:
Issa and colleagues survey the many types of adeno-associated virus, or AAV, used to carry new genes into the body, in a 2023 overview. Gene therapy aims to treat disease by fixing or replacing faulty genes. AAV carriers are a favored tool because they can reach many tissues and rarely cause disease themselves.

The paper walks through the main AAV types and what each does best. It covers the tissues they target, how long they act, and the hurdles that remain. Readers new to gene therapy get a clear guide to the carrier menu doctors choose from.
europmc-pmc10014083:
Bobrovitz and a large international team review how well past COVID infection protects against the Omicron variant, in a 2023 study. They also review hybrid immunity, the mix of protection from both infection and vaccination. The review looks at how strong that protection is and how long it lasts.

The authors pool past studies and use a method that tracks change over time. They focus on protection against Omicron infection and against severe disease. The results matter for vaccine timing and for public health planning, and the paper states its methods in careful detail.
europmc-pmc10133283:
Gao and colleagues test whether ChatGPT-written research abstracts can be told apart from real ones, in a 2023 study. They gathered abstracts from five leading medical journals and asked ChatGPT to write new ones on the same topics. The question was whether detectors and human experts could spot the fakes.

Blinded reviewers and detection tools each tried to sort real from generated text. The study reports how often each method was fooled. The results feed a wider debate on trust and honesty. They also bear on AI use in science writing.
europmc-pmc10373083:
Gu and Hübschmann built a software package in 2023 to tame long gene result lists. A common gene test returns the shared themes in a list of genes. The output can run to scores of terms with much repeat content. Past tools grouped the terms, but left repeats or uneven groups.

Their new method, called binary cut, splits a term map step by step. Gu tested it on fake and real data sets. Terms inside each group stayed close kin, while groups stayed apart. Meaning-based scores worked best with the method in their tests. The package, simplifyEnrichment, also draws charts and sums up each group. It is free through the Bioconductor store for the R language.
europmc-pmc10987683:
Wang, Gessler, Zhan, Gallagher, and Gao review a virus used to ferry genes into patients in this 2024 paper. Adeno-associated virus is a small virus that rarely causes illness. Rebuilt forms of it can carry a healthy gene into tissues and keep it active for years. Seven such gene therapies have won approval so far.

The review explains the virus's biology and how engineers tune it to hit chosen tissues. It surveys trials across eye, brain, metabolic, blood, muscle, and heart diseases, plus cancers. High doses bring risks, the authors stress. These include immune reactions, liver harm, and a clotting disorder of small vessels. Making enough virus is also a bottleneck. The paper closes with ways to blunt immune attacks and cut side effects.
europmc-pmc1247383:
Patz and a working group warned that land use change spreads infectious disease in 2004. Farming expansion, logging, roads, dams, and irrigation all reshape habitats. Mining, wetland loss, and city growth add pressure. Each change can spark outbreaks or shift steady infections.

Side effects include forest fragmentation, pollution, poverty, and migration. Together they ease disease emergence in clear chains. The group built a systems model linking land choices to disease. They also ranked diseases most tied to ecological damage. Patz offers policy steps that treat land and health as one problem.
europmc-pmc1247483:
Inoue and co-authors measured fluorinated compounds in mother and cord blood in 2004. PFOS and kin coat plastics, electronics, textiles, and leather goods. They had been found in human blood before. Rodent work hints they may disturb development through thyroid effects.

Fifteen mother and cord blood pairs were analyzed with precise methods. Detection limits reached 0.5 nanograms per milliliter for PFOS and PFOA. The method paired liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry and online extraction. Inoue focuses on pregnancy as a sensitive window. Measuring both sides of the placenta shows what reaches the fetus.
europmc-pmc1281283:
Oken and co-authors studied fish eating, mercury, and infant cognition in 2005. Fish carries mercury but also brain-building fatty acids. The cohort held 135 mother and infant pairs in Project Viva. Mothers averaged 1.2 fish servings weekly in mid-pregnancy.

Mean hair mercury was 0.55 parts per million at delivery. Ten percent of mothers topped 1.2 parts per million. Infants took a visual memory test at six months. Higher fish intake tied to higher infant scores. The link grew stronger after adjusting for hair mercury. Each extra weekly serving added 4.0 points to the score.
europmc-pmc1434783:
Curcumin, the yellow pigment in turmeric spice, may help prevent cancer, but its safety at high doses was untested. Lao and co-authors ran a dose trial in 2006 with healthy volunteers. Each person took one dose of a standard curcumin extract. Doses rose from 500 to 12,000 milligrams across groups.

Seven of 24 people had mild side effects, with no clear link to dose size. Blood tests found no curcumin at doses up to 8,000 milligrams. Trace amounts showed in two people at the top doses. Lao concludes that even large single doses are well borne, and backs longer trials for cancer prevention.
europmc-pmc1435883:
Stem cells from bone marrow hold promise for therapy, but labs must grow them first. Bonab and co-authors asked in 2006 whether long growth in a dish ages these cells. They kept mesenchymal stem cells, a marrow type that can form bone and fat, for about 118 days.

Growth slowed with each round of copying. Telomeres, the caps on DNA ends, shrank from 9.19 to 8.7 thousand base pairs. The power to change into other cell types faded after the sixth round. Bonab concludes the cells age from the start of culture. Teams should use them early, while their stem traits last.
europmc-pmc1550283:
Gene activity webs can reveal which genes drive body weight. Ghazalpour and co-authors built such a web in 2006 from liver data of crossed mice. They grouped co-active genes into modules, then tied modules to 22 body traits.

Some chromosome spots, dubbed module QTL, perturbed whole modules at once. For a weight-linked module, the team modeled which genes matter using both those spots and each gene's web centrality. Genes that were both central and under a spot's sway predicted weight best. Ghazalpour argues that joining genetics with network maps can pinpoint the genes that steer complex traits.
europmc-pmc1634883:
Cells under mild protein-folding stress choose survival over suicide, and the choice is timed. Rutkowski and co-authors explained how in 2006. Stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's folding workshop, triggers the unfolded protein response, which opens both rescue and death paths.

Mild stress switched on all sensors of the response. But the death-promoting messages and proteins are intrinsically short-lived, while folding helpers persist. So death signals fade as the cell adapts, and rescue wins. Rutkowski found the same pattern in a genetic case of such stress. Timing of decay, they argue, structures the verdict.
europmc-pmc1877083: The zebrafish lysozyme C promoter drives myeloid-specific expression in transgenic fish. — a 2005 science paper on a fish immune-gene switch. It drives the myeloid expression. The paper is the switch study: the findings on zebrafish genes, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1885283: Arabidopsis TFL2/LHP1 specifically associates with genes marked by trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27. — a 2005 science paper on TFL2 gene marking. It finds the trimethylation link. The paper is the TFL2 study: the findings on Arabidopsis genes, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2074083: The production of malignant primary hepatic tumours in the rat by feeding dimethylnitrosamine. — a 2005 science paper on chemical-induced liver tumors. It feeds the dimethylnitrosamine. The paper is the tumor-feed study: the findings on hepatic ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2270283: The harvest plot: a method for synthesising evidence about the differential effects of interventions. — a 2005 science paper on the harvest-plot method. It guides the evidence synthesis. The paper is the harvest-plot guide: the findings on the method tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2547983: Support vector machines and kernels for computational biology. — a 2008 science paper on SVMs in biology. It guides the SVM kernels. The paper is the SVM guide: the findings on computational ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2571983: Endogenous VEGF is required for visual function: evidence for a survival role on müller cells a — a 2008 science paper on endogenous VEGF. It proves the VEGF requirement. The paper is the VEGF study: the findings on visual ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2579683: The role of endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition in cancer progression. — a 2008 science paper on endothelial-mesenchymal transition. It studies the transition role. The paper is the role study: the findings on cancer ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
