fo-sho-hing-tsan-king-beal-1883:
Samuel Beal translated the Fo-Sho-Hing-Tsan-King into English in 1883. It appeared as volume nineteen of the Sacred Books of the East. The text is a verse life of the Buddha by Ashvaghosha.

Ashvaghosha's Sanskrit Buddhacarita survives complete only in its Chinese translation. Beal rendered the Chinese version into English, restoring the poem to the West. The narrative runs from palace luxury to the night of enlightenment. Prince Siddhartha's renunciation, temptations, and awakening unfold in verse. Beal was a pioneer of Chinese Buddhist studies in Britain. His translation let Victorian readers follow the classic poetic life in full.
vairo-de-fascino-latin-1583:
Leonardo Vairo, an Italian churchman, published De fascino, on fascination, in Latin in 1583. Three books study the evil eye, the belief that a mere look can sicken children, spoil milk, or wither love. Vairo treats its species and causes with scholastic care and many examples.

He asks how a gaze could harm at a distance, and what spirits or humors might carry the harm. Learned medicine and demonology meet in his pages. The treatise became the classic early-modern study of bewitchment by sight. Few superstitions have so long a history or so wide a map. Vairo gives the evil eye its fullest Renaissance hearing, argued like a case at law.
van-dale-de-oraculis-ethnicorum-latin-16:
Anton van Dale, a Dutch physician and scholar, published his two dissertations on the heathen oracles in Latin in 1683. He asks how long the oracles of Greece and Rome truly lasted, and who really spoke through them. His answers demolished the reigning theory that demons had talked from the shrines.

Van Dale shows priestcraft at work. The oracles, he argues, were human frauds kept up for gain, and they ended with politics, not with Christ's birth. Fontenelle later popularized the argument in French, and the Enlightenment ran with it. Van Dale's Latin remains the source. Few scholarly books have so quietly rearranged what educated Europe believed.
smith-use-and-abuse-freemasonry-1783:
Captain George Smith, an artillery officer and provincial grand master, published The Use and Abuse of Free-Masonry in London in 1783. Smith writes as an insider with a warning. His treatise distinguishes true Masonry from its false forms, criticizing lodges that had drifted into feasting, faction, or worse.

The critique is pivotal because it comes from within the Craft's own leadership. Smith calls for reform in the working of late eighteenth-century English lodges. His standards are discipline, charity, and knowledge of the ritual's meaning. Reform talk across the lodges took shape under his influence. The Use and Abuse remains the sharpest insider's diagnosis of what ailed Georgian Masonry, written by a man who wanted it healed.
plos-pone-0004883:
Hiroki Sugiura and Michael Dickinson measured generation of forces and moments during visual evoked steering in flying Drosophila, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sideslip, long term force, rolling moment, and pitching moment generated by tethered fruit flies were measured during optomotor reactions within an electronic flight simulator. Forces and torques were acquired by optically measuring angular deflections of a sensitive sensor as flies attempted steering maneuvers.

Precise force records decode fly flight control. Insects adjust forces within milliseconds of visual change. Robotics borrows such agile strategies. Tethered assays reveal natural aerodynamics. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004983:
Animals flash ornaments to advertise their quality. Why should rivals or mates believe the ad? Gary Bortolotti and colleagues tested one answer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The classic idea involves testosterone and immunity. They focused instead on physiological stress. Stress is measured through the hormone corticosterone.

Their results show stress mediates the honesty of social signals. Only birds in good condition can afford the full display. The stress hormone links body condition to ornament quality. That keeps the signal truthful. The study supports a physiological basis for honest advertising. It refines a long-standing debate in behavioral ecology.
plos-pone-0005083:
People judge health from faces. Skin color carries much of that judgment. Ian Stephen and colleagues tested the cues in PLOS ONE in 2009. They let participants manipulate calibrated face images. The controls changed skin blood perfusion and oxygenation color. Other participants then rated the faces for health.

Faces with richer blood color and oxygenation looked healthier. Skin blood state depends on cardiovascular and hormonal health. Our eyes read circulation as a health signal. Other primates use similar signals for dominance and status. The finding shows a deep perceptual habit. It may explain why illness so visibly pales the face. It also matters for designing health displays and avatars.
plos-pone-0005183:
The hearing cortex of the brain is laid out in fields that respond to sound, much like keys on a piano. Less was known about how other features of sound, or focused attention, change those maps. Woods and colleagues used brain scans to study the question in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Volunteers heard sounds while the team recorded activity with functional magnetic resonance imaging. The maps showed that sound features and attention both reshape how the cortex responds. Hearing, in other words, is not passive intake. The brain edits incoming sound, and this work shows where that editing takes place.
plos-pone-0005283:
Glucocorticoids are stress hormones that rise in wasting illnesses, and muscle melts away in those states. Part of the loss may come from eating less rather than from the hormones directly. You and colleagues separated those two factors in rodents in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team gave high glucocorticoid doses, restricted food, or both, then measured muscle energy use and protein metabolism. Separating the factors shows how much damage each one does on its own. That split matters for feeding and drug plans in patients losing muscle. When a sick man or woman eats less, the muscle loss that follows can slow their cure. So care teams need to know which share of the loss food can and cannot fix.
plos-pone-0005883:
Konika Banerjee and co-authors tested in 2009 whether general intelligence exists in a small New World monkey. In humans, scores across many mental tasks rise and fall together, defining the trait called g. Almost nothing was known about whether other primates show the same pattern.

Cotton-top tamarins took a battery of cognitive tasks, and individuals' scores correlated across domains. That is evidence for g beyond humans. A shared factor in a distant primate suggests deep evolutionary roots for general intelligence. The study opens comparative work on how such a factor arises and what it costs.
plos-pone-0005983:
Common spelling changes in DNA each shift cancer risk by a little. Lydia Quaye, Jonathan Tyrer, Susan Ramus and colleagues hunted such changes for ovarian cancer in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study tests variants across ninety-four candidate genes or regions in women with the invasive epithelial form of the disease and in women without it.

Known strong risk genes explain only part of family risk, so the search turns to these weaker, common variants. Testing so many candidates at once sets a fair bar for which links are real. The work feeds the slow build of a risk map for ovarian cancer, one that may one day guide screening for women at higher risk.
plos-pone-0006083:
Knowing how hard malaria strikes a place guides where control money goes. Laveta Stewart, Roly Gosling, Jamie Griffin and colleagues offered a faster gauge in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tests age-specific sero-conversion rates, blood markers that show past infection, as a rapid way to assess malaria transmission in a community.

Bugs and blood smears, the older gauges, are slow and costly to gather well. Antibody patterns by age can be read from a single survey round. A rapid local estimate lets health teams focus bed nets, spraying and drugs where transmission truly runs hot, a gain for countries where malaria money must stretch far.
plos-pone-0006183:
Staring at a pattern for a long time changes how the next pattern looks. Kai-Markus Mueller and colleagues studied this effect, called visual adaptation, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Brain cells that sense tilted and curved lines are thought to be basic building blocks for seeing shapes and objects.

Long exposure to such lines produces two after-effects that feel linked at first glance. The team shows the two effects can come apart, so they rest on partly separate processes. That split tells vision scientists that one simple fatigue story cannot explain adaptation. It refines how labs should test early shape vision in the brain.
plos-pone-0006683:
Rachel M. Brown, Edwin M. Robertson, and Daniel Z. Press studied learning and aging in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some mental abilities clearly decline as people grow older. Memory for facts and events is known to weaken with age. Less clear is how aging affects learning a new skill. The authors focused on sequence skill acquisition in healthy older adults.

Participants practiced a sequence task, and the team tracked off-line learning. Off-line learning means gains that appear after practice ends, often after rest. Comparing younger and older learners showed where aging changes the process. The findings help separate normal aging from disease in skill learning. They also inform how training might be timed for older adults.
plos-pone-0006783:
Traude H. Beilharz and her team pinned down how small RNAs mute gene messages in mammal cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The small RNAs are microRNAs. They latch onto gene messages and cut how much protein gets made. They also trim the tail at the end of the message. A short tail is a step toward the message being destroyed.

The team asked how much that tail trim, called deadenylation, does the muting. Their tests show the trim is a true part of the act in mammal cells. With its tail cut, the message breaks down fast. Less protein gets made as a result. Knowing the steps helps those who build RNA drugs.
plos-pone-0006883:
Andreas Kurth and colleagues reported a cowpox outbreak in zoo animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cowpox virus infections are described as an extremely rare zoonosis. Cases in Germany are nevertheless increasing. The virus is rodent-borne with a broad host range. It carries the largest genome of all poxviruses.

Banded mongooses and jaguarundis fell ill in the outbreak. Human infection followed after a time delay. The delay shows how animal outbreaks can precede human cases. Zoo settings bring exotic species and keepers into close contact. Tracking such outbreaks protects both collections and staff.
plos-pone-0006983:

Four female skulls carried signs of the infection. The evidence was both in bone shape and in molecules. Finding the disease in ancient remains pushes its known history back in the region. It also shows desert peoples long lived with this parasite.
plos-pone-0007083:

plos-pone-0007183:

plos-pone-0007283:

plos-pone-0009683:

arxiv-2606-16383: Bigger isn't always better. 21434-letters-of-edward-fitzgerald-to-fa:
Edward FitzGerald wrote to the famed actress Fanny Kemble for over a decade, and the letters are gathered in this volume. William Aldis Wright edited the set, first issued in 1895 and again in 1902. The first letters came from the publisher George Bentley, who had printed some in a magazine.

Mrs Kemble gave the rest to Wright in 1883, the year the flow of letters ends. Notes explain the many names and hints that fill FitzGerald's chatty pages. Readers meet the poet of the Rubaiyat in private mood, witty and warm. The book adds much to what is known of his last years.
arxiv-2601-06983: Ji Tong Wang and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers hybrid bound states in the continuum beyond diffraction limit. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Bound states in the continuum (BICs) have greatly impacted our ability to manipulate light-matter interaction at the nanoscale. However, in periodic structures, BICs are typically realized below the diffraction limit, thus leaving a broad spectral domains largely unexplored. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07183: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Zehai Yang and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers RAIRS. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. IVF is one of the most widely used ANNS (Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search) methods in vector databases. The idea of redundant assignment is to assign a data vector to more than one IVF lists. For reducing the chance of missing true neighbors in IVF search. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07383:
Research by Fabian Schnelle and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with igusa stacks for certain abelian-type shimura varieties. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors construct Igusa stacks for the good reduction locus of.

A class of abelian-type Shimura varieties that can be defined in terms of a PEL datum. Under the assumption that it is of type (A even) or (C) and unramified at a prime p p. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-08283:
Heba Shakeel and three co-authors present AgriLens for searching agricultural texts by meaning. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses the growth of unstructured text across domains. Large text collections need scalable ways to organize, summarize, and retrieve what they hold.

AgriLens unifies three tasks: interpretable topic modeling, zero-shot topic labeling, and topic-guided semantic retrieval. It uses BERTopic to extract semantically coherent topics from agricultural corpora. Zero-shot labeling names topics without hand-built training sets for each theme. For farmers' advisors, researchers, and extension services, topic-guided search could surface the right guidance faster. The framework keeps topics readable, so users can judge what a search result covers.
arxiv-2601-07683:
Akash Halder, Amlan K. Roy, and Debraj Nath study hydrogen-like ions inside a deformed version of quantum mechanics. They solve the Schrödinger equation for a Coulomb potential with a Dunkl reflection operator present. The Dunkl framework adds reflection terms to standard calculus. The authors give formulas for eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, and radial densities for ions with atomic numbers one to three.

They also discuss how energy degeneracy changes with and without the reflection. Degeneracy means several states sharing one energy, a hallmark of hydrogen-like systems. Tracking it shows exactly what the Dunkl deformation alters. Quantum information measures and statistical complexity of these ions are part of the study. The paper speaks to mathematical physicists testing how far standard results survive deformation.
arxiv-2601-07783:
Chaoyi Lin Yang, Gabriele Dessena, and Oscar Bonilla-Manrique build a cheaper way to record vibrations from unmanned aircraft on the ground. Structural vibration testing checks dynamic behavior, reliability, and structural integrity. Such tests need accurate data acquisition systems to capture acceleration well. Commercial systems with the right performance are often expensive and complex. Their 2026 preprint presents an affordable alternative for UAV taxi vibration testing.

Taxi tests roll the aircraft on the ground to excite its structure. Small research teams need data quality without aerospace-level budgets. A low-cost system widens who can run these tests. The design targets small-scale and experimental applications that commercial gear prices out. Aerospace engineers and university labs are the readers. The paper treats cost as an engineering requirement, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-07883:
Indrajit Sen and Matthew Leifer draw testable predictions from an alternative formulation of quantum theory. The formulation is local, scale invariant, and non-Hermitian, built on pilot-wave ideas. Pilot-wave theory guides particles with a wave, in the de Broglie-Bohm picture. Sen and Leifer use Weyl's definition of the gravitational radius of charge. From it they obtain a fine-structure constant for non-integrable scale effects. Their 2026 preprint explores the experimental predictions that follow.

Alternative formulations matter when they predict something different from standard theory. A concrete prediction gives experimenters a target. Scale effects that cannot be integrated away would leave specific signatures. The authors work out where those signatures should appear. The paper serves scholars in quantum foundations. It moves a new formulation from formalism toward the laboratory.
arxiv-2601-07983:
A 2026 preprint models how Earth's radiation record would change if the Sun met a cold interstellar cloud. Geologic records of cosmogenic beryllium-10 are sensitive to the radiation environment over time. Recent work suggests the Sun sometimes encountered massive cold clouds. Such clouds could compress the heliosphere to within Earth's orbit. Earth would then face increased galactic cosmic rays and energetic particles of heliospheric origin.

Beryllium-10 in ice and sediments is a natural archive of past radiation. Modeling the cloud encounter tells scholars what spike to look for. A confirmed spike would date a dramatic event in the Sun's recent travels. It would also test models of the heliosphere's protective bubble. The paper serves space physicists and paleoclimate scholars. It connects deep-space conditions to traces readable in Earth's own records.
arxiv-2601-08383: Bo Wang and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on where a model gains its facts in pre-training. The paper sets dense designs, where all parts work on each token, next to Mixture-of-Experts designs, where a few parts work on each token. That split lets size grow past dense caps, yet how it shapes the gain of facts was not known. The team sets out Gated-LPI, a neuron-level score based on log-probability increase, which splits gains across neurons.
arxiv-2601-08783:
Eline Kempkes and Alberto Perez de Alba Ortiz work on ways to map the energy hills of small scale systems. Such maps show which states a molecule likes and how it moves. Biased runs can cross hills that plain runs can not cross in time. But each new system tends to need fresh hand tuning of the bias.

The team boosts a known bias method called umbrella sampling. They add a math tool that sums the biased runs with less waste. The aim is a method that works well on many kinds of systems with less fuss. A reader who runs molecule sims gets a more firm path to energy maps. Less hand tuning means more time on the science.
arxiv-2601-08983:
Yinon Spinka and Oren Yakir study fair matches between random points and grid points on a vast graph. The graph is of a type that spreads fast, called non-amenable. Points fall at a set rate, at random. A match pairs each random point to a grid point. A good match keeps most pair spans short, and looks the same from each node.

The pair ask when a best such match can be built, and how short its spans can be. Past work left gaps for this fast spread graph type. Their work fills part of that gap with firm bounds. A reader in chance and graphs gets a new base case. It helps work on fair load share in vast nets.
arxiv-2601-09183:
Takahito Kashiwabara bounds how fast the flow strength can grow for the sea and air flow rules used in weather work. Those rules are the primitive equations. They run in a box that wraps round in the flat ways, with set rules at top and base. Full drag terms are kept in the rules, as in real flow.

He proves the strength gauge can grow at most by a single exponential in time. That bound is more sharp than past double bounds for this case. It rests on care with the top and base rules. A reader in flow math gets a firm growth cap. Such caps help prove that weather sims stay sound over long runs.
arxiv-2601-09583:
Berke Ates, Philipp Schaad, Timo Schneider, Alexandru Calotoiu, and Torsten Hoefler build tooling for people who design compiler languages. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents MLIR-Forge, a modular framework for language smiths. Domain-specific languages rely on custom middle forms inside their compiler pipelines.

Each new form adds power but also bulk, so it must be tested with care. MLIR-Forge aims to make building and testing such forms easier within the MLIR project. Good compilers sit under most computing in science, so better tooling lifts many fields at once. The framework targets the gap between a language idea and a reliable compiler.
arxiv-2601-09683:
I. F. Herrera-González computes how heat flows through a disordered chain of atoms. The 2026 arXiv paper studies one-dimensional harmonic chains with mass disorder and weak bond disorder. The chain's ends touch heat baths through weak, mismatched links.

The model includes correlations within the mass disorder, within the bond disorder, and between the two. An analytical approach, rather than pure simulation, reveals how those correlations steer thermal conductivity. Tiny chains are testbeds for the physics of insulation at small scales. The results inform how disorder can be used to block or guide heat.
arxiv-2601-09883:
Xinxing Ren and seven co-authors, from the CORAL project, replace fixed workflows for agent teams with information flow. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes an orchestrated multi-agent paradigm built on agent-to-agent communication. Most current systems follow workflows that engineers enumerate in advance.

In rule-based designs, humans must predefine task states, routing rules, and what context each step receives. That rigidity breaks on open-ended work. Letting agents pass information directly to each other promises teams that can adapt as their tasks unfold step by step. The new paradigm targets the brittle middle layer of today's agent frameworks, where most designs tend to break first.
arxiv-2601-10083:
Shayan Hamidi Dehshali, Tzu-Hsuan Liao, and Shaileshh Bojja Venkatakrishnan lay out links for vast fleets of low orbit craft. Such fleets can form a fast web with wide reach. Laser links let craft talk at high speed with low lag. But which craft should link to which is a hard call.

The team shapes the link web by demand. Places with more need get more links. The plan uses shape math and graph tools. It is tested in sims of the fleet. The aim is a web that serves real need, not a plain grid. That should lift speed where users are.
arxiv-2601-10283:
Dmitrii Kolotkov, Anne-Marie Broomhall, Laura Jade Millson, and Sergey Belov track sun waves past a cut off tone. The sun rings with sound waves from its core. Past a set tone, waves can leak to the air. Their hues show a fine comb of peaks and dips.

That comb comes from waves that clash as they rise. The team ask if the comb shifts with the sun's cycle. The cycle is the slow swing in sun spots and flares. They use both sun data and like data from far stars. A shift would tie deep waves to the cycle's pull.
arxiv-2601-10383:
Marcel Gohsen and co authors test if a busy mind misses fake voices. Fake voice tools can forge a speech with ease. Such fakes can spread false tales on social feeds. How well a hearer spots them sets how far a fake can go. Past tests used calm hearers with full focus.

Real hearers are oft busy or tired. The team ask if that load cuts spot rates. They test hearers under set loads as they judge clips. A drop would mean fakes gain when minds are taxed. The work speaks to how feeds and news rooms should flag voice clips.
arxiv-2601-10583:
Maximilian Schiffer, Heiko Hoppe, Yue Su, Louis Bouvier, and Axel Parmentier survey a young field that joins two older ones. The field mixes machine learning with combinatorial optimization, the math of choosing the best option from a huge set. It goes by the name COAML. The authors map its base ideas, its uses, and its open fronts.

In COAML, an optimization oracle sits inside the learning pipeline. The learned rules stay data-driven, yet they respect hard limits on what counts as a valid choice. The survey ties the field to machine learning, operations research, and stochastic optimization. It gives new readers one place to see the whole landscape and where work is still needed.
arxiv-2601-10883:
Andrea Rondelli designs a public-key cryptographic algorithm meant to stand against quantum adversaries. In antiquity, a seal stood for trust, secrecy, and integrity in letters. Modern public-key systems play that role for digital messages. Quantum computers threaten many of them, since they can break the math that current keys rest on.

Rondelli's design draws on differential geometry and algebraic topology for its hard problems. Geometry-based hardness is a less worn path than number theory. The paper frames the scheme as a bid to keep the old seal's promise in an era of quantum machines and strong AI. Cryptographers get a fresh candidate to test, attack, and judge.
arxiv-2601-11783: Murtuza N. Shergadwala tests a common way to audit AI systems in firms. In fields such as hiring, firms must show that AI tools obey set rules. A quick route is to let a large model judge if outputs obey the rules. That route scales well, but its steadiness was not checked. He calls the risk the stability trap. A judge that shifts its calls from run to run can hide real faults.
arxiv-2601-12183:
Davide Rinaldi, Radim Filip, Dario Gerace, and Giacomo Guarnieri chase max precision in charging multi-qubit quantum batteries. Precision, robustness, and efficiency all matter in quantum tech design. A charger must hit a set charge level, hold it under noise, and waste little energy.

They show that true quantum traits, plus non-Gaussianity, can give the best of all three at once. Their setup draws on a light-matter model. A precise quantum battery would help small quantum devices. The work maps how to reach that charge point.  Three goals at once is the hard core of the claim.
arxiv-2601-11383:
S. Giappichini, M. Klute, M. Presilla, X. Zuo, and M. Cepeda plan Higgs measures at FCC-ee. Their 2026 preprint studies the Higgs decay to tau pairs. The Future Circular Collider is CERN's planned flagship machine. Its electron-positron arm is called FCC-ee in the plan.

The tau-pair decay has a large share of Higgs decays. It is clean to spot in the FCC-ee setting. Tau polarization can also be rebuilt from the decay. Polarization adds a handle on the Higgs's traits. The team measures the cross-section for that channel. Such measures test if the Higgs acts as theory says. The work feeds the case for the future collider.
arxiv-2601-11483:
Lukas Vierus and coauthors extend tensor field tomography to moving fields. Their 2026 preprint handles attenuation and refraction at once. Tomography rebuilds inner fields from rays that cross them. Tensor fields carry direction as well as size at each point.

The model uses attenuated ray transforms of the fields. Rays bend along geodesic curves set by refraction. The bending follows a Riemannian metric from the refractive index. Time-dependence adds a dynamic case to the classic setup. The team derives adjoint operators for that dynamic case. Adjoints are the key step toward rebuilding the fields. Numerical experiments test the theory on synthetic data.
arxiv-2601-11683:
Zhuoyi Shang and five coauthors attest model lineage after fine-tuning. Their 2026 preprint tracks knowledge evolution along the tuning path. Fine-tuning creates lineage links among deep learning models. A tuned model descends from its base in a clear line.

Lineage could answer pressing security concerns in open libraries. Unauthorized redistribution of models is one such concern. False claims of model provenance are another live risk. Open-weight libraries often lack robust lineage checks. The team uses the fine-tuning trajectory as evidence. Consistent knowledge evolution along it attests true descent. Proven lineage helps owners prove what is theirs.
arxiv-2601-13083:
L. F. Melo, O. Jimenez, and L. Neves set sharp bounds on a core trade off in quantum tests. A test rig can split a quantum bit, called a quanton, across many paths. One part of the test shows wave like acts. A second part stores clues about which path was taken.

In their rig the quanton can take N paths, each as likely as the next. It meets a detector whose clue states are set in a fair, matched way. The team then proves bounds that link two scores. One score is wave coherence, read by a form of entropy. The other is path clue, read by shared data from telling detector states apart. The bounds make the old wave versus bit trade off exact for this broad rig.
arxiv-2601-13183:
Sergio Servantez, Sarah B. Lawsky, Rajiv Jain, Daniel W. Linna Jr., and Kristian Hammond build a new kind of test for law sense in AI. Tests of sense have driven gains in language models. Yet a fixed set of question and answer pairs gives just a snap shot. It squeezes rich acts into one score.

That flaw bites hard in law, where rules bind each step. Past law tests cost a lot to build and sort flaws poorly. Their tool, OpenExempt, is a probe test for law sense. They also give a frame to build like tests on call, fit to a flaw a team wants to isolate. Law and AI teams gain a way to find where a model fails, not just that it fails.
arxiv-2601-13283:
Abhinava Chatterjee and Chao-Xing Liu study how a surface effect can make sound like waves in a film act one way. The film is a magnetic topological insulator, a stuff whose bulk blocks current while its face can carry it. Wake its face states with magnetism and a half quantum Hall act shows on the face.

That face act is a mark of axion type charge rules. The team asks how it pairs with phonon Hall viscosity, a trait that can give sound waves a handed spin. They find face led chirality and one way acts for such waves. For staff who hunt new wave tools, one way sound in a film is a rich prize.
arxiv-2601-13383:
A. A. Jafari, C. Ozcinar, and G. Anbarjafari built a light frame for AI agents that firms can bend to their needs. Large language models sparked a shift in agent build. Agents can now sense, plan, and run multi step tasks. Yet old frames are oft stiff, tied to one vendor, or too bulk to bend fast.

Their frame, shown in a tool called AgentForge, is modular. Parts can be swapped with no tear of the whole. That keeps build light and lets teams test fast. For firms that must ship agents on a clock, a frame that bends beats one that must be fought. The paper lays out the plan, the build, and uses.
arxiv-2601-13483:
Louiza Fouli, Kuei-Nuan Lin, Haydee Lindo, and Maral Mostafazadehfard mark when the special fibre ring of a ladder module is Gorenstein. A ladder module is a sum of ideals of top minors of a ladder matrix, a matrix with a stair of zeros. Its special fibre ring codes how the module acts at a prime.

Gorenstein rings are a prized class with a deep duality. The team gives terms that are both need and apt for that trait. The terms are read off the matrix data that sets the module. For algebra staff, a read off test beats a case by case hunt for a trait as deep as this one.
arxiv-2601-13583:
J. Stiles built a Python tool kit to grade radio antennas in the frequency domain in one flow. Such tests check how an antenna takes power, beams it, and holds its tune. Data comes from both lab marks and sims, in mixed forms that take hand work to join.

The kit is called AAFIYA. It runs S parameters, impedance, realized gain, beam patterns, and polarization marks in one pass. It also gives a calibration based yield call, how many built units pass. It reads stock Touchstone files and beam data. For radio teams, one flow for all marks cuts the glue code each new test now needs.
arxiv-2601-12383:
Ahmad Mousavi and three co authors work on a hard class of optimization problems. The task is to shrink a smooth function, which may be nonconvex, over a sparse symmetric set. Sparse means most values in the answer should be zero. Sets of this kind show up in tasks where one wants a compact, clean solution.

The team put forward an improved penalty decomposition algorithm. It uses a quasi Newton method to solve a chain of penalty subproblems. The chain splits into two blocks with distinct traits. The first block has a closed form answer with no sparsity rule. The second block is handled by a fast sparse projection onto the feasible set.
arxiv-2601-12583:
The CMS Collaboration combines many searches for heavy new particles at the Large Hadron Collider. The quarry is a heavy vector boson resonance, a short lived particle with spin one. The data come from proton proton collisions at an energy of 13 TeV. Single searches each cover one decay path, and each has limited reach on its own.

The team merge the searches into one combined statistical analysis. The resonance could decay into pairs of W or Z bosons, or Higgs bosons. It could also decay into quark pairs or lepton pairs of several kinds. Combining channels sharpens the net limit on such a particle. A null result still pays off, since it rules out wide zones of theory space.
arxiv-2601-12683:
Liwei Liao and Ronggang Wang work on segmenting scenes built from 3D Gaussians. Such scenes represent a place as a cloud of soft Gaussian blobs. Segmentation methods for these scenes have emerged as the format spread. Most of them cut the scene at the level of single Gaussian primitives.

That primitive level cut has a flaw at object edges. Gaussians vary a lot in scale, and large ones often span foreground and background. Cutting by primitive then yields jagged boundaries on segmented objects. Their method is called GaussianTrimmer, and it trims boundaries online. Cleaner boundaries matter for editing, robotics, and virtual scene work. The work targets a visible artifact that users notice at once.
arxiv-2601-12983:
Jesus-German Ortiz-Barajas, Jonathan Tonglet, Vivek Gupta, and Iryna Gurevych test how language models can be misused to make misleading charts. Multimodal models now automate chart generation from data tables. That enables efficient analysis and reporting at scale. It also introduces new misuse risks, since a chart can lie while its data stay true.

Their framework is called ChartAttack. It evaluates how models can be prompted to generate misleading charts at scale. Slanted axes, cherry picked ranges, and swapped colors are classic chart tricks. Knowing how easily models produce them helps set guardrails. The work serves data literacy and AI safety at once.
arxiv-2601-13683:
Boyuan Cao and co-authors aim to cut the cost of making images with diffusion transformers in 2026. These models, called DiTs, make high-fidelity images that look sharp and true. Their self-attention step, though, grows in cost with the square of the input size. That quadratic cost blocks use at large scales.

The team builds a linear form of attention with a dynamic differential twist. Linear cost grows in a straight line, not a square, with size. Keeping image quality high while costs drop is the core test. Cheaper, finer image models would serve more users on less hardware.
arxiv-2601-13883:
Cuong Le, Thang Vu, Stefano Andrenacci, and Symeon Chatzinotas study spectrum sharing between ground and space networks in 2026. Terrestrial base stations and non-terrestrial ones, on satellites, must coexist in the same spectrum. Their joint resource allocation is a constrained problem. Real cases bring many channels, many users, and fast-changing user behavior.

The team uses constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning for the task. Many agents learn to share while respecting hard limits. Scale and flexibility are the twin aims of the work. Good sharing lets satellite links boost, not jam, ground networks.
arxiv-2601-14183:
Francesco Mottes, Qian-Ze Zhu, and Michael Brenner tune exact stochastic kinetic models with gradient methods in 2026. Such models describe systems across biology, chemistry, and physics. In them, events are discrete and counts are small, so smooth approximations fall short. Design and inference both need search over paths drawn by the standard sampler.

The discrete reaction events in those paths block the usual gradient flow. A gradient needs a smooth slope, and a jump has none. Their method finds a way to push gradients through such jumps. That opens exact models to the same fast tuning used in deep learning. The method runs on data drawn from past runs, with no fresh shots on the rig.
arxiv-2601-14283:
Kangyu Zheng, Kai Zhang, Jiale Tan, and a team across several labs compare drug design methods in this 2026 paper. The field is structure-based drug design, where new drug candidates are shaped to fit a target protein. Three kinds of algorithms lead the field. They are search-based methods, deep generative models, and reinforcement learning.

Most past studies compare models inside one kind only. Cross-kind comparisons are rare, so no one knows the true trade-offs. The team built a benchmark that runs all three kinds on shared ground. Its title says the results expose key trade-offs among 1D, 2D, and 3D methods. Readers get a fair map of what each approach does best.
arxiv-2601-14383:
Jennifer N. Stafford and four co-authors study heat flow in galaxy clusters in this 2026 paper. Cool core clusters have dense, cool gas at their centers that should cool and flow inward. Conduction, heat carried by particle motion, was mostly discounted as the fix. It moves heat too slowly to warm the core from outside.

The team looks at a special case. Jets from the central black hole can stir hot and cold gas into close contact. Conduction grows strong when materials of very different temperature sit that close. Their title calls the effect self-limiting. The paper studies how jet-modulated conduction behaves under that limit.
arxiv-2601-14483:
A. Mummery studies black hole masses in this 2026 paper. Tidal disruption events happen when a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and is torn apart. They offer a truly unique, and potentially very powerful, probe of the quiescent supermassive black hole population. Most black holes are quiet, so such probes are rare and prized.

Current survey capabilities shape what can be learned. The vast majority of tidal disruption events found in the next decade will be observed only across optical and ultraviolet wavelengths. Mummery studies mass inference from the optical flares of these events. Readers get a method to weigh dormant black holes from the flash of a single destroyed star.
arxiv-2601-14583:
Walter H. Hartung, Wei Chang, Sang-Hoon Kim, Taro Konomi, and Ting Xu write practical notes on RF cavity tests in this 2026 paper. Radio-frequency cavities power particle accelerators. A cavity with a mismatched input coupler poses a measurement problem. Direct calculation of power dissipation and intrinsic quality factor from continuous-wave measurements may carry uncertainty from systematic errors.

The authors focus on two-port CW measurements. Their notes cover self-consistency assessment: checks that tell whether the numbers agree with each other. They also cover indirect methods for the same quantities. Readers who run cavity test stands get guidance on trusting their quality factor values.
arxiv-2601-14683:
Aisvarya Adeseye, Jouni Isoaho, Seppo Virtanen, and Mohammad Tahir work on privacy in qualitative research in this 2026 paper. Qualitative data often contain personal, contextual, and organizational details. Those details pose privacy risks if not handled appropriately. Manual anonymization is time-consuming and inconsistent. It frequently omits critical identifiers.

Existing automated tools tend to rely on pattern matching or fixed rules. Such tools fail to capture context and may alter the meaning of the data. The team uses local language models for context-aware adaptive anonymization of sensitive text. Local means the text never leaves the researcher's machine. Readers get a privacy tool that reads for meaning before it hides a name.
arxiv-2601-15483:
Kahn Rhrissorrakrai and six co-authors test quantum machine learning on a medical task in a 2026 arXiv paper. The task is to predict antibiotic resistance from clinical urine cultures. Resistance ranks among the top threats to human health, the authors note. Poor antibiotic use is a main driver of that threat. Better prediction could guide treatment choices.

The team calls their study the first large-scale test of its kind. They check whether quantum methods help on this real clinical problem. They also study a data complexity signature. Per the title, that signature predicts when quantum projected learning gives a benefit. For clinicians and model builders alike, the draw is practical. The work asks where quantum tools earn their keep, using data from actual patient care.
arxiv-2601-15683:
Baradhwaj Coleppa, Akshat Khanna, Santosh Kumar Rai, and Agnivo Sarkar hunt for new particles at the LHC in a 2026 arXiv paper. Extending the scalar sector is a standard route beyond the Standard Model. Their model is the Three Higgs Doublet Model, with a Z3 symmetry. They work in the Type-Z, or democratic, Yukawa setup. The paper examines how this model would show up in collider data.

Their focus is neutral scalar cascades. A heavy scalar can decay through lighter ones in steps. Such chains leave distinctive signatures in detectors. Mapping those signatures tells experimentalists what to search for. It also tells them which signals would point to three doublets rather than two. For collider phenomenology, that translation from model to signal is the core service.
arxiv-2601-15983:
Masashi Aiko and five co-authors compute corrections to Higgs boson decays in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their model adds a complex triplet field to the Higgs sector. Such an extension can generate neutrino mass through the Type-II seesaw mechanism. The extension usually predicts a rho parameter different from one at tree level. Rho measures a key electroweak ratio. Its shift changes how electroweak parameters are renormalized.

That makes the model differ from the Standard Model and from two-Higgs-doublet models. The authors compute radiative corrections to decays of the 125 GeV Higgs boson in this setting. Precision Higgs data from colliders can then test the model. Small deviations in decay rates would be the tell. The paper supplies the theory numbers those tests need.
arxiv-2601-15183:
Marcelo Campos and Cosmin Pohoata update lower bounds for multicolor Ramsey numbers. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a classic question in graph theory. A Ramsey number marks the size at which a pattern must appear, no matter how edges are colored.

The work builds on results by Conlon, Ferber, and Wigderson, and on a step by Sawin. The key tool is an upper bound on how sparse the independent sets of a certain graph must be. From that bound, the authors draw fresh lower bounds for the multicolor Ramsey numbers.
arxiv-2601-15283:
Ruofan Liang, Norman Müller, and co-authors take indoor lighting apart so it can be remixed. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with light editing in indoor scenes. The input is a single multi-view capture of a room.

Their method uses a generative model to split the scene's light into its sources. Each lamp or window becomes a separate factor. Once split, each source can be edited on its own. Users can switch it off or on, shift its color, or change its brightness, and then rebuild the newly lit indoor scene at will.
arxiv-2601-15383:
Krista Lynne Smith, Macon Magno, and Michael Koss watch a small galaxy's core flicker in two bands at once. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with UGC 6728, a dwarf Seyfert galaxy. They present radio and X-ray light curves taken at the same times over five years.

The X-ray curve shows a flaring stretch, then a slow rise and fall. Through all that change, the X-ray hardness ratio and spectrum stay much the same. The observations were serendipitous, a lucky catch. Paired curves like these are rare for such a small active galaxy.
arxiv-2601-16083:
Matthew Shorvon, Frederik Mallmann-Trenn and David Watson tackle a core task in chance based thought. Their 2026 preprint deals with the best single guess for a set of facts. That guess is known as the maximum a posteriori pick. To find it in full is known to be hard. It stays hard in many plain cases and with rough methods too.

The team frames the task in a looser sense. They ask for a pick that is close to best with high odds. That frame is known as prob ably approx i mate ly correct in the field. A loose but firm frame can make hard tasks usable. The work sets bounds for when such picks can be found.
arxiv-2601-16383:
Soumitri Chattopadhyay, Başar Demir and Marc Niethammer test big med image tools with loose prompts. Their 2026 preprint deals with tools that cut 3D med scans by prompt. Such tools show strong skill when prompts are sharp. Real prompts in wards are oft loose or off the mark. Loose prompts may bend the cut in ways past tests miss.

The team bends dense prompts in set, ruled ways. They then weigh how cuts shift as prompts stray. Firm tools should hold their cuts through small prompt flaws. Weak tools will need prompt guards in real use. The work maps prompt risk for ward use.
arxiv-2601-16783:
Sam Mathew sorts all ways to morph one least-area graph skin to the next. A least-area skin spans a wire loop with least size. A graph skin is one drawn from a height map. Morph maps shift one height map to a next one. Their 2026 preprint gives a full sort of such morphs.

The sort lists which least-area graph skins can morph at all. It names the morph maps that do the job. Full sorts close long hunts in surface math. They also tell film and design tools which skins can blend. Least-area skins show up in roofs and nano forms too.
arxiv-2601-16983:
Willem Hoogendam and a large team read light from a comet born past our Sun. The comet 3I/ATLAS is just the third such guest known. Guests like it carry stuff from far star homes. Its gas glow can tell what that stuff is. Their 2026 preprint reads its glow since it passed the Sun.

A field scope split the comet's glow by place and hue. Past reads tracked it as it came in. Now it leaves, and its glow has shifted. Shifts tell how Sun heat changed its ice and dust. Such guests give rare ground truth on far systems.
arxiv-2601-17083:
Goldy Ahuja and Shashikiran Ganesh track how faint forces bend a comet's path. The comet 3I/ATLAS is the third known guest from past our Sun. It passed its near point to the Sun in late 2025. Now it heads out, set to pass near Jupiter. Forces past gravity's pull can nudge its path. Heat jets and light push are such faint forces.

Their 2026 preprint weighs how each faint force bends the track. The Jupiter pass sits at a third of an Earth-Sun span. True tracks tell if the comet's jets push hard or soft. They also sharpen charts of its home-bound path.
arxiv-2601-17383:
Chen Ling and five co-authors show a new attack on large vision-language models. These models see images and reason about the real world. Prompt injection is a known flaw, where fake commands hijack the model. Past attacks need access to input channels. Or they need to know the user's query. Those terms rarely hold in real use.

The team's physical prompt injection works in the open world. Malicious cues sit in the scene the model views. That makes the threat far more real for robots and cameras. Defenders must now guard the scene, not just the text box. The work sets a harder bar for safe deployment.
arxiv-2601-17483:
Barak Or tackles sudden failure in neural network training. Modern training can be fragile. Rare bad updates can cause divergence that cannot be undone. Or they can quietly drag quality down. Most current methods try to prevent such breaks inside the optimizer. Once a break starts, they offer little way back.

Or proposes automatic stability and recovery for training. The system should catch instability as it starts. It should then restore a sound state and resume. That shift treats training like a process that needs a safety net. Big training runs cost vast sums. A recovery tool could save runs that now are lost. The work targets a pain every large lab knows.
arxiv-2601-19683:
Hanting Niu and four colleagues improve a basic neural network tool. Multi-layer perceptrons are the standard blocks for learning functions from data. Their outputs are inherently smooth everywhere. Some real functions, though, are continuous yet have sharp corners at chosen points. Such functions are non-differentiable at those points by design, and smooth networks struggle to copy them.

Their network, SharpNet, is built to represent functions with controlled non-differentiability. The sharp features are prescribed in advance, so the model knows where the corners belong. Older workarounds bolted on fixes after training. A built-in ability should give cleaner and more exact fits. Shape modeling and geometry processing are natural homes for such functions.
arxiv-2601-20183:
Yuhua Zhao, Tiejun Lv, and Ke Wang study data freshness in satellite Internet of Things systems, where sensors send readings through orbiting links. Satellite links face long delays, fading signals, and scarce bandwidth all at once. A layered retransmission scheme improves reliability, but its backward decoding makes the age of the data unclear.

The authors define a metric that handles this ambiguity and use it in a cross-layer optimization. Their goal is to balance freshness against transmission efficiency, since sending more often wastes scarce bandwidth. The work matters for remote sensing networks, where stale data can be nearly as bad as lost data.
arxiv-2601-20283:
Tanmay Karmakar and three colleagues show that a single well-chosen word can fool a neural text ranking model. Ranking models are effective at retrieval, but earlier work showed they can be pushed around by attacks. The authors revisit this with a minimal, query-aware attack that promotes a target document.

The attack inserts or swaps in one word aligned with the query, the query center. If one word can lift a document's rank, ranking systems are more fragile than their scores suggest. The finding matters for search engines and for any contest where placement brings money or attention.
arxiv-2601-20483:
Ashot Matevosyan, Frank Jülicher, and Ricard Alert study noise that emerges in active gels when detailed balance is broken. In equilibrium, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem ties thermal fluctuations to dissipation. Living systems are driven out of equilibrium by internal processes, which produce extra, active fluctuations.

Predicting the statistics of those fluctuations is still hard, though they matter for functions such as transport inside cells. Active gels are lab models of the cell's inner scaffolding. The authors work out how nonequilibrium noise arises there, a step toward reading cell mechanics from its flickering.
arxiv-2601-18383:
Zhenyuan Guo and six colleagues look for a way to make large reasoning models cheaper to run. Such models write out a long chain of thought before they give a final reply. That chain helps on hard tasks, but it eats up memory and time. Long chains slow each reply and raise the cost of each run.

The team treats some parts of the chain as more key than the rest. Their plan picks which thought steps to keep with care. It trims the parts that add little to the final reply. A leaner chain should keep most of the skill while it cuts the load on the chip. Work of this kind is key as firms try to serve more users with the same stock of machines.
arxiv-2601-18483:
Arya Labroo and four colleagues test how well language models can hold two style goals at once. A user may ask for text that is both funny and strong in its pitch. Past tools could set one trait at a time, by prompt tricks or by tweaks inside the model. Joint sets of traits were far less checked, and the checks that do exist stay coarse.

The team built a finer test that grades traits one by one and in pairs. It asks if a gain in one trait costs a loss in the next. The title gives their main hint: the two goals tend to clash. A tool that must be both at once may end up as not quite each. The test could help firms set fair hopes for style control in chat tools and ad tools.
arxiv-2601-18683:
Alicja Polanska and Jason McEwen hone a way to score how well a world view fits the facts, in the hard case where the view has more than one peak. That score, called the marginal likelihood, sums the fit of a view over all its dial sets. It is the key score when two views are set side by side. It is also hard to work out when the peaks are far apart.

A past tool learned to fix the score from a set of draws from the view. It worked well but could wobble on peak-rich views. The pair blend it with a way to build draws that can hop peaks with ease. That blend should keep the score firm where the old tool shook. Firm scores help staff pick the right view of the sky, of genes, or of markets.
arxiv-2601-21483:
Jonas Becker and a large team build multilingual datasets for a richer kind of stance analysis. Classic stance work sorts a writer's view on a target into broad camps like favor or against. Real attitudes, though, vary in strength and heat, not just in side.

The team models stance along two smooth scales drawn from emotion science. One scale runs from negative to positive, and the other from calm to active. Their datasets cover several languages. Finer scales let researchers track how public feeling shifts in degree, which blunt labels can miss entirely.
arxiv-2601-21583:
Tin Hadži Veljković, Erik Bekkers, Michael Tiemann, and Jan-Willem van de Meent give learning systems a smooth way to predict sets of unknown size. Many tasks need a set as output: objects in a scene, molecules, or sources in the sky. The count is part of what must be predicted.

Older methods pad outputs to a fixed size or guess the count as a separate step. Both routes are clumsy and error-prone. The authors build continuous representations of discrete sets, so learning can flow smoothly. A cleaner set representation helps detection, science, and design tools that think in collections rather than single answers.
arxiv-2601-22283:
Giacomo Marocco, David Moore, and Daniel Carney set out a way to feel tiny pushes past a known quantum limit. Their 2026 preprint works with a tiny glass sphere held in light, free of any touch. The plan squeezes the sphere's state in all three directions of space.

A chain of quick jumps in the trap's rate does the squeezing. The team then weigh how real-world noise, called decoherence, caps the gain. Sharper push sensors could test weak forces and faint signals. The work shows what a real setup must beat. It is a clear target for labs.
arxiv-2601-22383:
G. Alencar, C. R. Muniz, and M. S. Oliveira map a black string in a curved cosmos onto a simpler field, twice over. A black string is a black hole stretched along one line. Their 2026 preprint works in anti-de Sitter space, a cosmos with a steady inward pull.

The trick, called the classical double copy, turns gravity math into gauge-field math. They cast the string in Kerr-Schild form over a drum-shaped base space. From that form they build the single copy and the zeroth copy. The work tests how far the copy trick reaches. Each new case firms up the claim.
arxiv-2601-22783:
Ilyass Moummad and a team speed wildlife record search by packing text codes into compact hypercubes. Biodiversity platforms hold vast archives of sightings, sounds, and notes. Their 2026 preprint notes that rich foundation-model codes make search slow at that scale, due to high-dimensional matching.

Compact codes cut the cost of finding like records. Fast retrieval helps trackers spot trends and rare events in time. The work serves field science with a systems fix. It keeps meaning while shrinking size. That trade is the whole game at archive scale. The gain grows as the archive grows.
arxiv-2601-21883:
Victor Spitzer and Francois Sanson study decision-focused learning, where a predictive model is trained to improve the final decision, not just its own accuracy. The model feeds a combinatorial optimization problem, such as scheduling or routing, and training must pass gradients through that optimizer.

That differentiation is the central challenge, and recent methods use perturbation-based approximations to get through it. Those approximations can make solutions jumpy, so this 2026 preprint focuses on managing solution stability, using cost regularization to keep decisions steady. Stable decisions matter in practice. A delivery plan that flips wildly after small data changes is hard to trust. The same holds for a power schedule.
arxiv-2601-20683:
Samuel Rhys Cox, Joel Wester, and Niels van Berkel study how chatbots should give feedback. Their paper appears in the 2026 CHI conference proceedings. Chatbots are now common in programs that help people change habits. The tone of a bot's reply can shape how users react. A style that feels pushy can spark reactance, the urge to push back.

The team frames a design trade-off. Feedback must not feel like a threat to the user's freedom. Yet it should still surprise and engage the user. A polite style may be safe but dull, as the title hints. The study weighs these two pulls against each other. Its lessons help designers pick a voice for bots that coach health and habits.
arxiv-2601-20783:
Naveen Durvasula proposes a principled way to order transactions in smart contracts. His 2026 paper presents the Monotone Priority System. Modern blockchain applications gain from stating sequencing constraints on the calls they receive. Order can decide who profits and who loses. But free-form constraints could make block production hard to compute.

Durvasula seeks a balance between expressivity and tractability. The system lets contracts specify how their function calls should be sequenced. It does so on an axiomatic basis, so the rules rest on stated principles. The aim is a design that is both flexible and practical for block builders. The paper speaks to blockchain designers who need fair, predictable ordering without slowing the chain.
arxiv-2601-21083:
Jarrod Barnes measures whether AI incident responders know when they might be wrong. The 2026 paper presents OpenSec, a benchmark for incident response agent calibration. As language models improve, so do their offensive uses. Frontier agents now generate working exploits for under fifty dollars in compute, he notes. Defensive agents must keep pace. Existing benchmarks, though, conflate doing an action with doing it correctly. That hides calibration failures.

Calibration means the agent's confidence matches its true accuracy. The danger grows when agents process adversarial evidence. Attackers can plant clues that mislead the responder. OpenSec tests agents under exactly that pressure. It separates action execution from correct execution in scoring. The benchmark helps security teams judge which agents to trust at 3 a.m. It reframes defense evaluation around honest uncertainty.
arxiv-2601-21183:
Jacek Duszenko localizes the exact moment a reasoning model caves to its user. The 2026 paper studies sycophancy in reasoning models. These models frequently agree with incorrect user suggestions. That behavior is known as sycophancy. It is unclear where in the reasoning trace the agreement originates. It is also unclear how strong the commitment is. Duszenko introduces sycophantic anchors to answer both questions.

An anchor is a sentence that causally locks the model into agreement. Once written, the rest of the trace follows it. Anchors can be located and their strength quantified. That turns a vague worry into a measurable event. Developers could then target training at those sentences. The work serves anyone who needs AI that pushes back when the user is wrong. It gives sycophancy a handle researchers can grip.
arxiv-2512-01283:
Haifeng Yang and Lile Wang present a new code for tracking light in space. Light can be polarized, which means its waves line up in a set way. That pattern can reveal the shape of gas, dust, and fields around stars and black holes.

Their code, Kratos-polrad, runs on graphics cards to gain speed. It sends many test rays through a model scene and tracks how each ray bends and twists. The code keeps the twist of the light correct at each step. Fast and correct runs like this help teams test ideas about what a scope should see.
arxiv-2512-01583:
Nicola Fabiano proves a fixed point result in quantum metric spaces. In such spaces, distance between states is set by the L2 norm. Contraction maps shrink distances at each step. In classic spaces, they must hit one fixed point.

Fabiano shows the same holds in the quantum frame. He proves both existence and uniqueness of the point. He also argues the quantum frame has structural gains over fuzzy frames. Fixed point results back iterative methods used across physics, economics, and data science. The proof uses no extra compactness claims, which keeps its scope broad across the quantum spaces where such maps arise in practice.
arxiv-2601-22883:
Michiel De Wilde and Robert Seiringer show a surprising freedom in how an ideal Bose gas can condense. In such a gas, many particles settle into the lowest energy state, forming a condensate. With the right boundary rules for the space, the authors prove far more freedom is possible.

In the large-system limit, any number of condensates can appear, each shaped by an arbitrary harmonic function. Harmonic functions are smooth shapes fixed by a simple equation. The result widens what theory says quantum gases can do at very low temperatures.
arxiv-2601-22983:
Tristan Bilot, Baoxiang Jiang, and Thomas Pasquier build a fair testbed for intrusion detection based on system history. Such systems watch provenance graphs, records of which process touched which file, to catch advanced attacks. Comparing them has been hard because studies use mismatched data prep, splits, labels, and metrics.

Their tool, PIDSMaker, standardizes how these detectors are built and judged. A shared yardstick shows which methods truly work, and which only looked good under friendly settings. That clarity helps defenders pick tools that hold up in real networks. Standardized splits and labeling are part of the remedy, since mismatched ground truth made past comparisons nearly meaningless.
arxiv-2601-23183:
Casimiro Pio Carrino and four co-authors release JobResQA, a benchmark for reading résumés and job descriptions. It tests machine reading comprehension of language models on human-resources tasks. The set holds hundreds of question-answer pairs over synthetic résumé and job pairs in five languages.

Questions range over three levels, from basic fact extraction to cross-document reasoning. Multilingual hiring documents are a real test of practical language skill. A public benchmark helps employers and builders judge tools before trusting them with applicants. Synthetic résumé and job pairs keep the benchmark safe to share, avoiding real applicants' private employment histories.
arxiv-2512-00083:
Large language models need huge amounts of memory while they generate answers, which strains current hardware. Zhongchun Zhou, Chengtao Lai, and Wei Zhang present LLaMCAT in a 2025 conference paper. Their target is the last-level cache, the fast memory layer shared by processors in GPUs and AI accelerators.

LLaMCAT optimizes how that cache is shared and throttled during model inference. Better cache use can speed responses and lower the cost of running large models. The work matters as language models grow and memory, not raw computing power, becomes the main limit on performance. The paper appeared at a major parallel computing conference in 2025. Cache behavior is often where that memory limit bites first.
arxiv-2512-03183:
Heavy grains settle as they move in turbulent flow. Y. Zhang, D. H. Richter, and A. D. Bragg study that settling near walls in this 2025 work. Gravity gives grains a settling speed and also changes how they interact with the flow.

Wall direction matters, the authors explain. When a wall is flat, both effects push grains toward it. When a wall is upright, only the second effect acts. Knowing these rules helps predict dust, ash, and pollutant spread in pipes, rooms, and the atmosphere. Settling rules also affect how ash and dust coat surfaces in homes and factories.
arxiv-2512-03483:
Fluid equations with randomness need careful numerical analysis. Binjie Li and Qin Zhou study two-dimensional stochastic Navier-Stokes equations in this 2025 work. Their system includes transport noise and no-slip boundaries on a convex polygonal domain.

The main challenge is a lack of spatial regularity in the solution. That gap blocks standard error analysis techniques. The authors establish strong convergence rates for the spatial finite element discretization. Proven rates tell engineers how much to trust simulations of turbulent, noisy flows. Transport noise models how flows stir particles, a key effect in environmental fluids.
arxiv-2512-02083:
Domination problems ask how to place guards on a network so every node is covered, and the Roman variant lets some posts count double. Sangam Balchandar Reddy analyzes in 2025 the computational complexity of signed Roman domination, where vertices receive values that can also be negative.

A signed Roman dominating function must give every closed neighborhood a positive total weight while obeying rules at each vertex. Knowing whether finding the best such assignment is easy or provably hard guides algorithm designers. Complexity results like this sort network optimization problems into those worth attacking exactly and those needing heuristics.
arxiv-2512-02283:
Self-driving and other safety-critical machines increasingly explain themselves by recovering the equations that govern them, a technique called model recovery. Bin Xu, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep Gupta tackle in 2025 the problem of running that recovery on small edge devices, where memory and energy are tight.

The obstacle is the method's engine, neural ordinary differential equations, whose iterative solving maps poorly onto FPGA hardware. The authors adapt model recovery to survive those resource constraints while staying real-time. Explainable decisions matter most exactly where edge devices operate, in physical systems whose failures are dangerous and whose reasoning must be auditable.
arxiv-2512-02483:
Rozhin Mohammadikian and three co-authors ask whether news and ideas spread through social networks by chance. Online platforms now move posts faster and wider than ever before. If spread followed clear patterns, those patterns could be mapped and perhaps predicted.

Working with real world hashtag data, the team finds that spread is not random at all. Hashtags travel along preferred routes, following specific patterns as they move between users. Findings like these matter for anyone who studies rumors, campaigns, or viral posts, since the path a message takes shapes who sees it. That kind of map helps explain why some posts fade fast and some spread far and wide.
arxiv-2512-02683:
Luiz A. Rodrigues, Elias P. Duarte Jr., and Luciana Arantes build self managing broadcast trees for distributed systems. Sending one message to all processes by direct flood overloads the sender. A spanning tree spreads that load, passing each message along shared branches.

Their autonomic algorithm lets the processes build and maintain the tree themselves. When machines join, leave, or fail, the tree repairs its own shape. Self healing communication backbones keep large systems running through churn, a basic need for cloud services and sensor networks alike. A tree that heals on its own needs no crew on call, which is the whole point for far flung nets.
arxiv-2512-02783:
Björn Þór Jónsson and three co-authors ask what quality and diversity should mean when a computer explores sounds. Digital synthesis opens parameter spaces with millions of possible sounds. Quality diversity algorithms search such spaces well, but only if sounds are measured in the right features.

Handcrafted descriptors and trained classifiers can bias the search toward familiar sonic regions. The team explores definitions of quality and diversity inside sonic measurement spaces. Better measures could help sound designers and musicians discover genuinely new timbres, not just variations on sounds already known. What counts as a new sound is the hinge here. Set the bar by ear, by plot, or by rule, and the hunt takes a new path each time.
arxiv-2512-02983:
Louis McConnell and four co-authors map the neighborhoods of tumors so treatments can be tailored better. The spatial architecture of the tumor microenvironment shapes how cancer grows and responds. ProteinPNet learns from spatial proteomics data, which records many proteins across tissue locations.

Built on prototypical part networks, the framework discovers recurring microenvironment motifs directly. Unlike post hoc explanation tools, it learns interpretable spatial prototypes during supervised training itself. Faithful prototypes could help oncologists read a tumor's layout and choose therapy with the tissue context in view. A map of tumor hoods in plain forms gives drug teams a place to aim. A black box score can not give them that at all.
plos-pone-0010183:
The authors were Adam Anas, Joppe Hovius, Cornelis van 't Veer, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice to test a sensor in lung inflammation. Lipopolysaccharide, or LPS, is a molecule on Gram-negative bacteria that the body must sense to defend itself. Lab work suggested a protein called CD14 was needed to pass that signal onward.

The team induced acute lung inflammation with different LPS chemotypes, forms that vary in structure. They then checked how much CD14 mattered for each form in living mice. The answer shapes understanding of lung injury during severe bacterial infection.
plos-pone-0010283:
The authors were Kelly Tremblay, Kayo Inoue, Katrina McClannahan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked how repeated listening reshapes hearing in the brain. Auditory training programs are being built to help people with communication disorders. Training improves perception, and biological changes in the brain come with that improvement, raising interest in markers of progress.

The team exposed listeners repeatedly to sounds and tracked how brain encoding changed. If a brain signal marks training gains, clinics could measure progress objectively. Their results add to the science behind hearing rehabilitation and listening therapy design.
plos-pone-0009883:
Madagascar's mouse lemurs are tiny primates, and telling their species apart is tricky. David Weisrock and colleagues faced that problem where the usual genetic test fails. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mouse lemurs are among the smallest primates on Earth.

Delimiting species means drawing the lines between one species and the next. The usual test needs nuclear monophyly, a clean family-tree split in nuclear DNA. Without that signal, the team needed other evidence to draw the lines. Clear species limits matter for counting and protecting Madagascar's wildlife.
